item.title: Core Concepts in Infrastructure Cost Management
item.dc:creator: Doug Meil
item.description: There is a benefit to the clarity that comes with knowing what was racked and the associated costs.
item.content:encoded:
“All that glitters is not gold.” – William Shakespeare

“. . . but all that glitters and blinks must have a cost center” – Doug Meil

When discussing and comparing on-premise and cloud deployment patterns a decade ago, there would have been a straight line drawn from the first to the second: On-premise was the past and cloud computing was the future, even if people weren’t entirely sure what “cloud computing” was at the time. It is worth re-examining the strengths and weaknesses of both deployment modalities, especially given some notable movements back to on-premise deployments.

On-Premise Cost Management

At the risk of stating the obvious, “on-premise” in the context of this post refers to deployments either within an organization’s physical premises (office or datacenter) or a third party co-located commercial datacenter. Equipment might be purchased or leased, but being on-premise generally refers not just to bare metal servers, but to racks, cables, power supplies, top of rack networking, routers, cooling, raised floors, physical security, and everything else that goes with running a functioning and stable computing environment.   

On-premise deployments are sometimes viewed as inflexible and static; however, they can be quite adaptable when commodity hardware is paired with infrastructure as service frameworks and container frameworks for automated deployments of configurations and software releases. Being comparatively static is true enough as new equipment needs time to be provisioned, but the “static-ness” of the environment is point-in-time, not a permanent condition. The top environment management and scaling challenges are typically:

  1. Choice / Lifespan of Hardware
    1. Especially with purchased equipment, decisions regarding hardware (CPU/GPU, storage, networking) have years of impact, both in terms of technical solution delivery and financials (capital expenses, depreciation). 
  2. Dev and QA Environments
    1. Sizing a production environment is one matter, but properly sizing lower environments can be a challenge—specifically justifying the budgets and proposed/expected utilization to management.
  3. Shared Environment Management
    1. Data and analytic environments are designed to bring data together across sources and teams, but ensuring everybody gets their fair share of resources (and is appropriately paying for it) isn’t always easy. 
  4. Site Failover and Disaster Recovery
    1. This is a particularly hard problem because a fully built-out environment just sitting around waiting to get used is something that most organizations cannot afford. 
    1. This all too often turns into a paper exercise for most organizations.

There is a benefit to the clarity that comes with knowing what was racked and the associated costs. What you see in the racks is exactly what you have.

Cloud Cost Management

Given the complexities of managing on-premise environments, it can be tempting to assume that moving to the cloud will be an easier path because someone else can manage the infrastructure. As with so many things in life the answer is “it depends,” and it especially depends on which pain points are prioritized and which specific cloud features are being leveraged. There is truth in the saying “the cloud is just somebody else’s computer,” but this does not adequately capture the complexity of public cloud platforms like Azure, AWS, and Google Cloud, which are not merely a sets of servers in somebody else’s datacenter, but a vast array of services, many of which are provided by the cloud platform vendor, and some are provided by third parties.   

How does one manage a cloud environment? As with on-premise deployments, looking at costs is a good place to start and the major cloud platforms have built-in cost management dashboards. Below is a screenshot of Azure Cost Analyzer from documentation: 

There are a lot of great numbers and graphs in this dashboard, so it might seem at first glance that our cost management problems are solved. Let’s take a look and find out. 

Service Utilization

Looking closer at the example screenshot provides a useful summary of services, providing a stack-rank of cost categories: Virtual Machines in first place, and Storage in second place. This is useful insight, but this also raises further questions: 

  1. Virtual Machines. Money is clearly being spent on compute, but on how many VMs? What are they doing? Are they fully utilized? 
  2. Storage. “Storage” in cloud computing can mean everything from local storage to VMs to cloud storage services, and charges can be accrued for writing, storing, and reading data. What exactly is being stored where, and at what cost? Storage services also have optional replication and redundancy capabilities available for up-charges.

None of these initial questions address how well this cloud-hosted solution is functioning. Performance diagnostics and tuning are enormous topics outside the scope of this post, but should still be mentioned because they wind up invariably having a cost impact somewhere. So many questions from a single pie chart! Getting access to diagnostic logs, as well as detailed billing records, are highly recommended for deeper analysis.

It should also be clear by this point that pretty much all the core on-premise challenges still remain in the cloud, but there are just a more tools that can be brought to bear. One construct is to configure appropriate “resource groups” around services and provisioned resources, which can align on major groups of functionality for solutions. Such reporting can be seen in the lower right-hand corner of the high-level cost dashboard, though in the example data nearly all the costs are rolling up to a single resource group.  Resource and activity tagging can also be used for more detailed breakdowns (e.g., function = ABC, department = XYZ).

First-generation cloud deployments generally looked like the above and consisted primarily of VMs and and storage. Today, however, higher-level services are often driving the largest expenditures—especially data and analytic services (for example, Databricks and Snowflake)—and this presents another level of management and observability requirements. A fundamental challenge when building with cloud services is that it is often difficult to know exactly how much something will cost. While cloud services offer flexibility, they also introduce a level of complexity that is under-appreciated.   

Understanding the difference between actual costs vs. amortized costs also matters. Cloud resources and services can often be purchased (or reserved) in blocks with discounts. This can be useful where workloads requirements are better understood, but it also increases complexity of reporting with respect to “cash out the door” vs. reserved resource/service utilization. 

Service-Detail Utilization

To understand what is happening within any given cloud service will require access to service-specific activity and billing records, as well as a thorough understanding of the constructs of the service. Using Databricks as an example, there are major service components such as:

  1. Unity Catalog — the overarching catalog for assets (data and code).
  2. Compute — classic compute for notebooks, which execute in the customer account and accrue cloud VM and Storage charges plus Databricks runtime charges, and “serverless,” which executes entirely in the Databricks control plane but at a higher rate of Databricks runtime charges. 
  3. SQL Warehousing — classic (customer account), serverless.
  4. AI functions — SQL functions, Genie spaces for LLMs, coding assistants, etc.

As all of this may execute entirely within a single cloud resource group, proper tagging becomes critical to differentiate activity and billing from a variety of teams, workloads, and stages (for example, Dev/QA/Prod). Otherwise, developers and administrators will be flying blind. The cost summary of the service will be visible, of course, but that isn’t enough to manage a solution, much less an enterprise rollout.

Adding to the pressure is that it often is not easy to see what cloud-based solutions cost until they have been built. Service-level utilization analysis and tagging is truly a skill within a skill. 

Haven’t We Been Here Before?

Today people can joke about a server running under someone’s desk, but up until roughly the 1980s that would have been highly aspirational, if not science fiction. In the very old days, computing time often was leased on shared systems because only the largest organizations could afford not just to own their own computers but also to build out and operate datacenters to house them. Owning and operating one’s own computing environment represented not only a significant strategic advantage for purpose-built systems, but also operational control and stability. There were good reasons on-premise systems deployments were preferred by so many, once they became economically feasible. 

Public cloud computing appeared in the late 2000s and took hold the following decade. When dynamic resource provisioning and scaling is combined with the wide breadth of services available, this modality can be an especially powerful paradigm. This, however, comes with the age-old tradeoff of vendor lock-in; if a cloud platform decides to raise the rates on a critical dependency, in the short-term there often isn’t much of a choice other than to absorb those costs.      

It should not come as a surprise, then, that there have been some notable examples in the “back-to-on-premise” movement. If workloads are thoroughly understood and predictable, on-premise deployments still can represent not only a cost-effective approach, but one with control down to bare metal if one so chooses. 

All of this, whether on-premise or in the public cloud, is part of effective FinOps (financial operational analytics). Whichever deployment path is taken, the responsibility of environment management never ends, and there are no free lunches.

References

1. Meil, D. Delivering Cloud Data and Analytic Solutions. BLOG@CACM (January 7, 2025).

2. State of Tokenomics: September 2026. FinOps Foundation.

3. Engro Technologies. Cloud Repatriation: Why Some Enterprises Are Moving Back On-Prem? LinkedIn.

4. Wikipedia. All That Glitters is Not Gold.

item.title: Another Proposal to Rename AI
item.dc:creator: Mario Antoine Aoun
item.description: A proposal to use Super Computer Intelligence as an alternative name for artificial intelligence.
item.content:encoded:
In this post, I introduce Super Computer Intelligence as an alternative name for artificial intelligence (AI), which also responds to U.S. President Donald J. Trump’s suggestion of renaming AI as Super Intelligence.

Etymologically speaking, “artificial” comes from the Latin “artificialis,” which breaks down to “ars” (that is, art, skill, or craft) and “facere” (that is, to make or do). In other words, it means “to do skill.” Intelligence comes from “intelligentia” (meaning understanding or discernment), derived from “intelligere,” meaning “to understand or comprehend.” Therefore, “artificial intelligence” merely translates to “understand skill making.”

Historically speaking, the term “AI” came to light through the Dartmouth Summer Research Project in 1956 organized by McCarthy, Minsky, and others.1 I argue that naming conventions are caught in social and historical contexts.2 In fact, McCarthy openly admitted that he preferred “AI” as a title for their summer project to avoid having to interact with or be overshadowed by Norbert Wiener, who cherished the term “cybernetics” instead. At the time, cybernetics (that is, control and communication in the animal and the machine)3 focused on mapping biologically inspired feedback mechanisms to analog hardware control loops, but McCarthy aimed for a naming convention that encapsulated logic, symbolic computation, and high-level programming. Historical reports4 indicate that McCarthy wanted a brand new captive name diverging from “automata theory” or “complex information processing” which could be more original and would attract financial backing. Later on, the name artificial intelligence would resonate well with Minsky’s theory of Society of Mind,5 which states that human intelligence can be considered as not a single, unified mechanism, but rather as an emergence born from the interactions of countless smaller, mindless parts called “agents,” which cannot think, feel, or understand but are manageable,5 hence can be engineered in a way that their outcome is attributed as artificial.

Philosophically speaking, the word “artificial” is the opposite of “natural.” For instance, an artificial flower contrasts a natural flower such that the former still shows beauty in its appearance, at least when seen from afar in perspective, but lacks the true nature of feeling, sensitivity, and appeal (beauty) found in a living flower when examined and touched closely. Thus one could argue that if we have called, or agreed upon, AI in its early beginnings, as computing, computer or machine intelligence, or intelligent machinery,6 then its ultimate expectations would never have existed because its technological wonders would have been known in simple practicalities as we may realize them now through image recognition, speech recognition, words sequence acquisition, etc. Simply saying, consider the facts that we have different kinds of intelligence (to name few: social intelligence, swarm intelligence, evolutionary intelligence, decentralized intelligence, biological intelligence, and neuro-symbolic AI), then we can notice with just a change of words that we can discreetly separate one kind of intelligence, those just mentioned, as one type of many others while not assuming that one is better than the other; they are all equal in terms of being intelligent in a way of at least solving a specific problem. In fact, all those forms of intelligence can be scaled and each one has its own limitations.

For example, Ant System7 inspired from ants’ decentralized colony intelligent behavior can solve the problem of finding a “good enough” optimal path from a food source to the nest. An ant colony fulfills such objective when scavenger ants find a food source and lay pheromones on such path; after that, all other ants will follow the same path and the whole colony is oriented towards the food source. This behavior has been translated to an algorithm and implemented in computer networks by directing data across Internet nodes that have minimal load or traffic.8 Therefore, ants can solve an optimization problem using decentralized intelligence; in such a framework there is no central server (such as a “big” ant directing the operations of the others), as each ant is following simple rules but the overall behavior of the whole colony is considered intelligent and their (the ants’) behavior is very efficient—intelligent—for such specific task.

In biological intelligence, the repository of knowledge and research is magnificent and endless. To name a few, we have synaptic plasticity, which helps us in building concepts and their associations by strengthening connections between neurons in the brain, as well as having dopamine levels that increase while we are anticipating an end goal. Those dopamine signals help us reinforce beneficial associations to achieve that goal.

Another example is evolutionary intelligence, where we have genetic algorithms mimicking the hereditary behavior of species’ chromosome crossovers and mutations in order to find the best fit (that is, the best solution) through many generations of mating. Such problems are challenging for humans to solve and their solution is promising using computer intelligence. Since all those forms of intelligence can be manifested and modeled using computers and acknowledging the fact that human intelligence would always be a peak endeavor, then why can’t we simply call their attempts as computer intelligence and therefore free us from the artificiality of the name artificial intelligence?

Finally, while writing this post, U.S. President Donald J. Trump, speaking before the United Nations General Assembly on September 22, 2026, requested references to AI be changed to “Super Intelligence” (SI) in all U.S. documents.9 However, that notion is missing an identifier because any intelligence can be superb, even human intelligence. Besides, if SI means beyond human, then that is impossible because there will always be areas where humans can excel while intelligent machines will be lacking. For example, if we hide the data we gather on Mars or the Hadron Collider from the machines, then “they” will never be able to surpass us in comprehending Martian matter or the bosons, respectively.

In addition, considering the fact that current state-of-the-art AI algorithms require super computing power, then one could suggest a fair name: Super Computer Intelligence. This preserves the super-computing-power condition that is required for AI to function properly and possibly beyond our expectations, as well as its fundamental ground that is computer intelligence, which is the basic naming right for it.

References

1. McCarthy, J., Minsky, M. L., Rochester, N., and Shannon, C. E. A Proposal for the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence, August 31, 1955. AI Magazine 27, 4 (2006), 12.

2. Derrida, J. and Spivak, G. C. Of Grammatology, Vol. 2, pp. 162-254. Johns Hopkins University Press, Baltimore (1976).

3. Wiener, N. and von Neumann, J. Cybernetics or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine. Physics Today 2, 5 (1949), 33-34.

4. Radanliev, P. Artificial intelligence: reflecting on the past and looking towards the next paradigm shift. Journal of Experimental & Theoretical Artificial Intelligence 37, 7, 1045–1062.

5. Minsky, M., & Lee, J. The Society of Mind, Vol. 1. Simon and Schuster, New York (1988).

6. Turing, A. Intelligent Machinery (1948).

7. Dorigo, M., Colorni, A., and Maniezzo, V. Distributed optimization by ant colonies. In Proceedings of the first European conference on artificial life (1991), pp. 134-142.

8. Di Caro, G. and Dorigo, M. AntNet: Distributed stigmergetic control for communications networks. Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research 9 (1998), 317-365.

9. UN News. Trump defends military action against Iran, Venezuela, and calls for rebrand of AI. United Nations.


Mario Antoine Aoun is an ACM Senior Member who has been a Reviewer for ACM Computing Reviews since 2006. He has more than 25 years of computer programming experience and holds a Ph.D. in Cognitive Informatics from Canada’s Université du Québec à Montréal. His main research interest is memory modeling based on chaos theory and spiking neurons.

item.title: Click Fraud Beyond Bots: Why Better Models Are Not Enough
item.dc:creator: Harshit Agarwal
item.description: Click fraud has persisted not because detection engineering is inadequate, but because the economic incentives surrounding it reward fraud at every layer of the supply chain.
item.content:encoded:
In 2024, advertisers lost more than $100 billion to digital ad fraud, and Juniper Research projects the figure will reach $172 billion by 2028.7 Click fraud accounts for the largest share of that loss,7 and absolute costs have climbed relentlessly even as detection has improved. Not because the fraud rate is rising, but because global ad spending has expanded faster than defenses. No other engineering problem of this scale, with this level of sustained investment, has resisted solution for this long. That should give the computing community pause—not about whether detection technology is improving, but about whether detection technology is even the right lever.

The field’s dominant framing—treat invalid clicks as a classification problem, train a better model, deploy it—is not wrong; it is insufficient. Click fraud has persisted not because detection engineering is inadequate, but because the economic incentives surrounding it reward fraud at every layer of the supply chain. Detection operates on one layer. The incentives operate on all of them.

More Bots, Broken Audits

DoubleVerify detected 140% more CTV fraud schemes in Q1 2026 than a year earlier, identifying over 50 distinct bot variants in 2025 alone.5 The newest of these are agentic AI bots that mimic human browsing—scrolling, hesitating, navigating—specifically engineered to defeat the behavioral signals that current detection relies on.5 The measurement problem runs deeper than the fraud itself. A March 2025 Adalytics report described by The Wall Street Journal found that Integral Ad Science labeled known bot traffic as human 77% of the time across a 2019 to 2024 dataset; DoubleVerify missed the same bots 21% of the time.1 DoubleVerify disputed the methodology and filed a defamation suit; a securities class action followed in May 2025.4 But the core implication—that MRC accreditation does not guarantee bot blocking—was not substantively denied. Advertisers paying for third-party verification may be receiving less protection than they believe, and the companies measuring fraud carry the same structural incentive to under-report it that platform operators choose to tolerate.

Three Actors, Three Motives, and One Misconfigured Detector

The field treats click fraud as a single problem. It is not. Three distinct actors commit it for entirely different reasons, each requiring a different detection approach.

The first is the platform operator: generating fake traffic through bot networks or click farms costs a fraction of building legitimate traffic, yet earns the same per-click rate. This is rational behavior given the incentive structure, not a technical failure. A classifier trained on this type of fraud will systematically miss the other two.

The second actor is the competitor. In high-CPC (cost per click) categories such as legal, finance, and real estate, a single click can cost $50 to $100,3 and fraudulent clicks can account for up to 30% of total traffic in these verticals.3 Competitors direct bots or click farms at a rival’s ads to deplete their daily budget, removing them from the auction entirely. A 2025 PPC study found that 50% of marketers attributed nearly half of their fraudulent clicks to competitor activity.3 This variant is particularly hard to detect: it originates from real devices, often in the same geographic market as a legitimate audience. The distinguishing signal tends to be post-click behavior—sabotage clicks bounce immediately, real buyers navigate and linger.

The third actor is the fraudulent affiliate. Affiliate networks pay commission per click or conversion, creating a direct financial incentive for commission theft. Industry estimates place affiliate fraud at approximately 17% of affiliate traffic, costing around $3.4 billion annually.10 The Honey.com controversy of 2024 to 2025 brought one technique—cookie stuffing—to mainstream attention: the browser extension replaced legitimate affiliate cookies at checkout, claiming commissions on purchases it had no role in generating.9 More broadly, affiliate cloaking rose from 25% of fraud cases in 2022 to 45% by 2024.11 The detection signal is the commission-to-conversion ratio: a fraudulent affiliate accumulates clicks that evaporate before any purchase completes.

A classifier trained on platform-operator bot traffic will miss competitor sabotage—real devices, no purchase intent—and affiliate fraud—real clicks, stolen attribution. One detection system cannot be equally calibrated for all three.

An Arms Race, Not a Classification Problem

Standard detection trains on known bad traffic and catches what resembles it. Click fraud breaks this: the moment you improve your filter, fraudsters study what gets caught and adjust until they slip back through. Your false-negative rate is their calibration target—they need not defeat your system, only stay outside your detection zone. In practice, this probing tends to leave a trace: test traffic clusters just below your detection threshold, and a sudden spike there is often the first sign someone is mapping your defenses. Sometimes days pass before false-negative rates move. Watching the shape of your score distribution—not just the overall filter rate—turns their reconnaissance into your early warning.

The response is to use multiple independent signals that are hard to defeat simultaneously. Three signals worth combining in practice: click timing variance within a session (bots are either too mechanical or too erratic); scroll depth before clicking (bots head straight to the ad unit; real users wander first); and navigation path entropy (bots take direct routes; organic users meander). Evading one is straightforward; evading all three requires sustained human mimicry that is hard to automate at scale. More fundamentally, the goal is not to raise the detection bar—it is to make it invisible. Any threshold a fraudster can locate becomes one they can calibrate against. Overlapping signals with randomized decision elements make the boundary much harder to find.

Agentic AI bots challenge this directly. A scripted bot fails behavioral detection because its timing is mechanical, its paths direct, its scroll behavior absent. An agentic bot is goal-directed: given the objective ‘appear human to this classifier,’ it can observe which sessions get flagged, infer which signals triggered detection, and adapt until it passes. The signals above were calibrated against bots that did not know what was being measured. An agentic bot can learn what is being measured. Timing variance, scroll depth, and navigation entropy each lose their discriminating power the moment the adversary can optimize against them directly. The implication is a shift toward infrastructure signals—network fingerprints, device consistency across sessions, hardware attestation—that operate below the layer a bot’s learned behavior can influence. The arms race does not end; it moves to a layer that is harder to fake.

Why the Supply Chain Cannot Fix Itself

The economics of programmatic advertising reward fraud at every level. When a fraudulent platform operator inflates traffic with fake clicks, their reported numbers—click rates and impression volumes—look better than those of an honest operator who cleaned theirs up. Advertisers following the best-looking metrics send more budget to the fraudster and less to the honest operator, penalizing exactly the behavior that should be encouraged. The middlemen—ad exchanges and supply-side platforms that route transactions between advertisers and platform operators—earn a cut of every transaction regardless of traffic quality, so removing a high-volume fraudulent operator directly hurts their own revenue. Nobody in the chain has a financial reason to fix the problem, and the players with the most visibility into traffic quality have the least incentive to use it. The only pressure that can break this comes from advertisers. Requiring independent verification before spending, and negotiating refunds for confirmed invalid traffic, shifts the cost of fraud back onto the intermediaries who profit from tolerating it.

Platform operators in court. The pattern is consistent across two decades: the entity with the most visibility into traffic quality has the strongest financial reason not to look too closely. Google settled a click fraud suit for $90 million in 2006.8 Meta faced a class action over invisible ‘stealth clicks’ charged at full CPC rates.2 In 2026, the FTC sued Amazon, alleging its algorithm extracted an estimated $20 billion from advertisers through artificial auction manipulation.6

When Traffic Quality Fights Revenue

Inside every platform, fraud filtering creates an organizational conflict. Removing fake traffic makes reported clicks and sessions fall—which shows up on dashboards as a revenue problem, even when filtering is working exactly as intended. Without a prior agreement, this tends to play out the same way: the fraud team tightens a threshold; the revenue team points to falling numbers; the threshold gets loosened. The fix is a pre-agreed filtering rate that both teams commit to before the quarter begins, a number neither can change alone. When the rate holds, the threshold holds. When it is breached, both teams investigate together. In my experience, this structural alignment matters more than any model improvement: a better model inside a broken organizational structure gets overridden back to the same bad result.

Fixing click fraud requires working on two fronts the industry has treated as separate. On detection: watch how the mix of filtered traffic changes, not just the overall rate; test against fraud the system currently misses, not just what it already catches; and keep the detection boundary hidden so adversaries cannot calibrate against it. On incentives: advertiser pressure for mandatory refunds on confirmed invalid traffic, and regulatory enforcement of the kind the FTC is now pursuing against Amazon. Detection catches fraud after it occurs. Changing incentives removes the motivation to commit it in the first place. Until the incentive front receives the same investment as the detection front, click fraud engineering will remain what it has been for two decades: always improving, never arriving.

Disclosure:  I used generative AI tools for limited editorial assistance, including language refinement and structural review. I independently reviewed and verified the content and references and take full responsibility for the final version.

2. ClassAction.org. Facebook Inflates CPC Ad Prices by ‘Stealth’ Clicking on the Ads Itself, Class Action Says. (2024).

3. ClickPatrol. PPC Click Fraud Study 2025: Key Statistics, Industry Insights, and Prevention Strategies (2025).

4. DoubleVerify Sues Adalytics, Jury Trial Demanded, MediaPost (May 16, 2025); DoubleVerify Class Action Lawsuit: Shareholder Portfolio Decimation After the Truth Emerges. ClassActionLawyerTN (2025).

5. DoubleVerify. Must-CTV: Streaming’s Shift From Promise to Performance (2026 Global Insights Report). Summarized in CTV fraud schemes up 140% as AI arms both sides of the fight. PPC Land (2026).

6. FTC sues Amazon, accusing the e-commerce giant of misleading advertisers. CNBC (August 31, 2026).

7. Juniper Research. Quantifying the Cost of Ad Fraud: 2023–2028. Research whitepaper (2024).

8. Google Agrees To $90 Million Settlement In Class Action Lawsuit Over Click Fraud. Search Engine Watch (March 8, 2006).

9. PPC Land. Honey drops to 14 million Chrome users amid ongoing affiliate scandal (2025).

10. TrafficGuard. The State of Affiliate Fraud in 2025 (2025).

11. Affiliate cloaking is behind 45% of fraud—here’s how to beat it. Search Engine Land (2025).

With over 14 years in the industry, research spanning marketplace monetization and agentic AI systems, and a first-place win at eBay’s company-wide Invent Week Hackathon, he specializes in large-scale platform engineering, monetization system design, and applied AI—shaping the commercial infrastructure of global online marketplaces.”

item.title: A Research Agenda for the Economics of Transformative AI
item.dc:creator: Erik Brynjolfsson
item.description: We urgently need to improve our understanding of AI’s economic implications.
item.content:encoded:
AI has improved radically in recent years and is poised to become more powerful. Our institutions, organizations, skills, and economic models are struggling to keep pace. In this growing gap lie the greatest risks and challenges of the coming decade, as well as the greatest opportunities. We urgently need to improve our understanding of AI’s economic implications.

Key Insights

  • Transformative AI (TAI) is advancing faster than our economic institutions can adapt, creating both unprecedented opportunities and significant risks that demand immediate attention.

  • The implications of TAI are affecting almost all areas of economics and are posing fundamental questions about economic growth, science and innovation, income distribution, decision-making power, geoeconomics, information and knowledge, safety risks, and even our sense of meaning and worth.

  • In this rapid transitional period, interdisciplinary collaboration between economists, computer scientists, and policymakers is crucial for developing the tools needed to align TAI with human well-being and prevent exacerbation of existing inequalities.

  • Traditional productivity measures and GDP miss AI’s full economic impact. New economic measures must be developed to understand and prepare for a rapidly changing and fundamentally different economy.

Before we can formulate effective solutions, we must define the fundamental questions, laying the groundwork for a productive research agenda. By doing so, we seek to catalyze the insights and analytical tools necessary to navigate AI’s evolving landscape while fostering shared prosperity. A question well-posed is half answered.

As rapid as improvements in AI have been, from mastering Ph.D.-level exams to writing essays and creating art, there are reasons to believe bigger advances will occur within the next few years. Timelines for achieving future AI milestones have accelerated. In 2020, the median prediction on Metaculus for the arrival date of a “general AI system” that could outperform most humans was 2062. As of mid-2026, the median prediction is May 2031, while a quarter of participants expect it to be achieved by May 2028.6

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in October 2024 that AI that exceeds almost all humans in almost all cognitive tasks might appear as soon as 2026,4 and Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis said in 2025 he expected it around 2030.28 While it is inherently difficult to predict dates for future inventions, we cannot dismiss the possibility that extremely powerful AI systems will be available within a decade.

Such powerful AI systems would transform society. Even current AI technologies have the potential to affect large sectors of the economy. An influential analysis estimates that current generative AI systems will significantly affect at least half of the tasks of 19% of workers in the U.S. economy, while 80% of jobs will have 10% or more of their tasks affected.15,a Looking forward, a report from the National Academies on AI and the Future of Work estimates that productivity growth rates could double in the coming years as a result of these technologies.31

More capable forms of AI would have broader and deeper effects. For example, interactions among AI agents could reshape the foundations of economic activity as they negotiate contracts, make investment decisions, and drive consumer choices. This dynamic interplay between AI and human agents is poised to redefine the economic landscape in ways we are only beginning to grasp.

The economic and societal changes are likely to unfold slowly at first, then rapidly.13 We urgently need a proactive research agenda to guide the redesign of our economic institutions, norms, and policies. We need to understand how to realize the potential of transformative artificial intelligence (TAI) while minimizing its risks.b

We present a research agenda here to motivate attention to critical questions about how TAI will impact the economy and societal well-being. Among the key concerns are how TAI will influence productivity and invention, as well as the extent to which it may exacerbate inequality or concentrate decision-making power. Other pressing issues include the interaction between TAI and global governance, implications for truth and misinformation, catastrophic risks, and ensuring economic incentives align with broader social welfare.

Our agenda is relevant to all researchers and policymakers interested in the broader effects of AI on society. Economics provides powerful frameworks for analyzing how transformative technologies affect society through production processes, resource allocation, and market mechanisms. Economists study how technologies such as AI change production functions—the relationship between inputs (labor, capital, data) and outputs—and how these changes ripple through markets, affecting productivity, wages, prices, and growth. Unlike technical analyses that focus on capabilities, economic analysis emphasizes societal outcomes: Who benefits, what trade-offs emerge, and how can institutions adapt to technological change?

Research on the economic implications of TAI can help policymakers craft better policies. This includes redesigning labor laws, tax systems, social insurance programs, antitrust and market regulations, as well as updating macroeconomic policies and global governance structures. A well-informed policy response will be essential to ensuring TAI creates broad-based prosperity rather than exacerbating economic division.

Our analysis employs an economic framework to systematically analyze how TAI will affect processes at multiple levels. This framework examines three interconnected dimensions:

  1. How TAI affects innovation processes and the creation of new ideas

  2. How TAI reshapes the organization of production factors through new business models, market structures, and institutional arrangements

  3. How TAI substitutes for or augments individual factors of production, particularly human labor and cognitive capabilities

This three-level approach helps structure our research questions and connects them to established economic methodologies.

What TAI Means for the Economy

Holden Karnofsky defines TAI as “potential future AI that precipitates a transition comparable to (or more significant than) the agricultural or industrial revolution,” including “some overlap with concepts put forth by others, such as ‘superintelligence’ and ‘artificial general intelligence.’”19 Like Karnofsky, we intend TAI to be a more comprehensive term, leaving open the possibility of AI systems that are transformative for the economy and society, despite lacking many abilities humans have. Conversely, TAI will exceed human capabilities on other dimensions, as existing AI already does.

While TAI could take many forms, for concreteness we highlight a potential manifestation Amodei calls “powerful AI,” which he summarizes as “a country of geniuses in a datacenter”:c an advanced AI model with intelligence surpassing the most capable humans across multiple fields, able to perform complex tasks such as solving mathematical theorems, creating novel works, or directing experiments autonomously. Millions of instances of such AI genius could run in parallel, each working 10 to 100 times faster than a human brain.

Despite its capabilities, powerful AI could be constrained by several bottlenecks, including a lack of physical embodiment, limits on the response times of physical systems or external software, requirements for computational infrastructure to support its large-scale operation, and policies. Such bottlenecks could hinder the speed and scale of its economic impact and should be a focus of analysis. TAI’s actual form may differ from the specific instantiation we describe here.

It is useful to monitor both technological and economic indicators that capture complementary aspects of the transition. We list both sets of indicators in the online appendix.

Grand Challenges and Key Questions

To effectively prepare for the development of TAI, we must first understand the key economic questions and challenges it presents. We identify nine Grand Challenges where economic analysis can shape TAI’s trajectory and impact. For each challenge, we define key research questions that need to be addressed (See Table).

We expand on each of these Grand Challenges in the ensuing nine subsections and pose additional research questions. Our goal is to inspire the research community to tackle these challenges and questions.

Economic growth.  Improved technological capabilities are the key drivers of growth in standard economic models.3 How can economists detect early signs of an AI-driven “growth explosion”14 improving upon approaches like those of Nordhaus?32

The nature of growth constraints is likely to change significantly. Current bottlenecks, such as limited supply of workers, human capital, and physical capital, may evolve or be supplanted by new limiting factors. Which bottlenecks will gain prominence in a TAI-driven economy, and how will these differ from traditional constraints? Will energy availability, computational resources, or raw materials become key constraints? Current frontier models require significant energy resources, rare earth minerals, and water for cooling. Research is needed to quantify these ecological constraints and model how they might affect the diffusion and economic impact of TAI.

The role of human capital is likely to undergo significant changes. How will the value and relevance of human capital evolve as TAI is developed? Which human skills will become redundant, and which are likely to remain in demand as TAI capabilities grow? How should education and training systems adapt to prepare workers?

The diffusion process will be crucial in determining how the benefits of TAI are realized and distributed. What factors will influence the rate of TAI adoption, and how will these affect economic growth? What policies could promote optimal diffusion of TAI?

Invention, discovery, and innovation.  Since innovation is the primary driver of economic growth, it is important to understand how TAI may transform the nature and extent of innovation.

How and where will TAI automate scientific discovery? Traditional innovation processes are costly and constrained by the time required to formulate hypotheses, conduct experiments, and iterate on solutions. TAI systems may dramatically reduce costs and time involved. How will the ability to automate experimentation and problem solving at scale influence the rate of technological progress? What are the likely bottlenecks? What will be the impact on the frequency and quality of innovations and, consequently, the rate of economic growth?

TAI may also affect the extent of disciplinary and non-disciplinary innovation. Many of the most transformative innovations emerge from the integration of knowledge across distinct fields, yet human cognitive limitations often prevent experts from identifying novel connections between disciplines. Many discovery-based institutions (e.g., universities and institutes) today are organized around disciplines, including training, promotion, and dissemination. To what extent will TAI, equipped with access to cross-disciplinary data and capable of synthesizing disparate knowledge, identify previously unrecognized complementarities? By generating insights that bridge domains, how might TAI impact not only the rate of innovation but the direction by shifting the innovation process from discovering local maxima (disciplinary discoveries) to more global discoveries (not constrained by disciplines)? What are the implications for economic growth?

Today, innovation is concentrated in firms and institutions with substantial resources and expertise. Will TAI democratize the innovation process? Will it allow small firms, entrepreneurs, and individuals to perform sophisticated innovation activities, including R&D, previously out of reach? Although humans may still need to articulate desired outcomes, will TAI be able to do most of the rest of the work of the innovation process? What will be the new bottlenecks?

To what extent will TAI shift the distribution of the agents that engage in the innovation process? Or will the production of innovation shift from human brains to compute? How will this impact the rate and direction of innovation? What will be the marginal value of intelligence itself? In what domains will frontier models be most valuable compared to less sophisticated types of AI?

Income distribution.  Labor is the main source of income for most of the population; therefore, labor markets play a crucial role in income distribution. Technological progress has traditionally gone hand in hand with both job displacement and the creation of new work, although not always in balance.2,5 Advances in AI may be far more rapid and transformative than earlier technologies.25 Simple economics suggests that if a machine is a close substitute for a worker in a job, the worker’s market wage will tend to fall to the cost of having a machine do the same tasks.

Will the capabilities of TAI largely displace workers, or will there be areas with rising labor demand? How might changing bottlenecks affect the distribution of economic gains across sectors and populations? How will this depend on economic policy?

If machines can perform essentially all work tasks, the remaining jobs may be either transitional or may involve demand for labor for intrinsic human-centered reasons.22 What will those jobs look like, including the balance between cognitive and physical work? What are the implications for equilibrium wages, employment levels, and unemployment rates? If compute and robots become close substitutes for labor, will they remain sufficiently scarce and expensive to preserve a significant role for labor?

The purveyors of TAI may earn significant gains from their inventions. Will this lead to an increase in income inequality in relative terms? Or will a growing economy lift all boats and ensure that the remaining labor demand is sufficient to spread around the surplus equitably? And how will these developments affect the concentration and inequality of wealth? How will these questions depend on whether AI systems are proprietary or open source?

Our existing social safety nets are designed around the notion that labor is the most important source of income. Social security and health benefits depend on people’s jobs or labor income. There is disability insurance for people who cannot work, and there is unemployment insurance for people who lose their jobs. Will our social safety nets still perform their role effectively in a TAI world? If not, how can they be adapted? What mechanisms of social insurance and income distribution can we design to ensure that TAI’s benefits are shared broadly across society?

Concentration of decision making and power.  There is an ongoing debate about concentration in the AI industry itself. The success of ever-larger models suggests the possibility that the AI industry may become increasingly concentrated, while the success of low-cost models of nearly equivalent performance and the success of open source models could support more competition.27 Will TAI be dominated by a single AI system, a small number of comparable systems, or a plethora of systems with varying capabilities and strengths?

Perhaps more importantly, how will TAI affect concentration in the rest of the economy? TAI and digital technologies change the cost of information processing, and as machine learning enables rapid analyses and application of previously tacit knowledge, economic organizations and institutions will also change. For instance, will larger retailers and manufacturers gain competitive advantage over small single-unit shops and plants? Will centrally planned economies find new life? Or will AI democratize expertise and lead to flourishing competition? More subtly, which types of information and decisions, if any, will become more centralized, and which types will become more decentralized, and under what conditions?

Relatedly, if TAI eviscerates demand for labor and drives down wages, as is contemplated in the preceding section, what will be the effects on the distribution of economic bargaining power? Will capital owners, who tend to be more concentrated than labor, become more powerful? Will governments or technologists or another group ascend? If so, how will they be governed?

As TAI enables more autonomous digital agents to participate in economic activities, questions of human agency and control become economically significant. Research is needed on the efficiency and welfare implications of delegating economic decisions to AI systems, the optimal division of control rights between humans and machines, and the design of mechanisms that preserve human autonomy while leveraging AI capabilities.

Furthermore, economic concentration often leads to concentration of political power. So, changes in the locus of economic decision making may ripple through to other parts of the economy. In particular, even if a highly centralized system optimizes more types of economic decision making, will it at the same time erode individual autonomy and liberty?

The political economy of AI regulation warrants economic analysis. Key questions include how concentrated AI development affects regulatory capture risks, how different regulatory approaches might impact innovation rates and diffusion patterns, and what governance structures could balance innovation incentives with societal risk management. Game-theoretic approaches could illuminate the strategic interactions between developers, regulators, and competing nations.

Geoeconomics.  Geoeconomics is an emerging field which examines the use of a country’s economic strength to exert influence on foreign entities to achieve geopolitical or economic goals. It involves leveraging economic instruments such as trade policy, investment, and sanctions to advance national interests.

TAI may have profound implications for geoeconomics, including military applications and their effect on global security, shifts in economic power due to productivity gains that are not uniformly distributed across states, international governance and regulatory frameworks, and challenges to political stability and information control within countries.

How will TAI reshape the economics of deterrence and the balance of power among states? How will TAI impact the stability of economic and military alliances and rivalries? Could TAI challenge traditional notions of nation-state power and enable small actors to wield significant influence, for instance, by creating an autonomous “army”?

How will TAI change the economics of cyber warfare and the defense of critical infrastructure? Can regulatory frameworks manage the dual-use nature of AI technologies without hindering economic growth?

Differential adoption of TAI could also exacerbate global economic inequalities between nations and affect trade flows. Will existing industrial capacity, research infrastructure, or policy frameworks determine which countries capture the most value? How might TAI reshape global trade patterns, particularly the competitive position of emerging economies? Will TAI alter the geopolitical importance of industries such as manufacturing, agriculture, and services, and how might trade policies evolve in response?

What policies can countries with limited technological capacity adopt to avoid marginalization in a TAI-driven global economy? How might global inequality affect the economic and political influence of technologically lagging states? What role can foreign aid or technology-sharing initiatives play in closing the TAI gap between countries? How will TAI-induced inequality affect migration patterns, regional stability, and global cooperation? How will TAI influence cooperation on shared challenges such as climate change or public health crises?

International governance frameworks for TAI could address geopolitical risks and ensure the technology evolves peacefully and benefits all countries. How can international institutions balance national sovereignty with coordinated oversight? How can the global community prevent regulatory arbitrage, where countries adopt divergent rules to gain competitive advantages? What factors influence whether major technology companies succeed in regulatory capture?

These geopolitical questions connect to broader discussions of digital sovereignty, including debates around digital tokens, data governance, and platform regulation. Economic research on TAI should build on existing work examining how digital technologies reshape political and economic power across borders.

Information, communication, and knowledge.  A key determinant of a society’s economic success is how it manages information, communication, and knowledge. Laws, institutions, incentives, and norms that promote the creation and transmission of accurate information tend to boost economic growth. For instance, the U.S. Constitution gives Congress the power to promote the progress of science and useful arts by granting authors and inventors exclusive rights to their writings and discoveries for a limited time. More broadly, the jury system, blind scientific reviews, libel laws, and the scientific method itself are systems intended to favor truthful information.

Digital information systems, communications, and social media are increasingly intermediated by AI-based recommender systems and populated by AI agents. False news has been found to spread farther and faster than the truth when amplified on social media.30 How will TAI affect the quality of information flows? How can we ensure the collection of information, performed for example by the media, is sufficiently compensated to create incentives for the production of high-quality information?

Relatedly, AI systems are creating content by themselves by processing information. How useful and innovative will this content be? Will it provide deeper and broader insights, even novelty? Or will it be misleading and destructive? AI-based deepfakes can misrepresent people and events. Could TAI simply overwhelm human-produced content with the sheer quantity of content it produces?

In the spirit of the preceding section, TAI may also affect political stability by enhancing the ability of states and non-state actors to manipulate information. What are its implications for authoritarian regimes, democratic governance, and social cohesion? How might TAI shape public opinion, disrupt political processes, or suppress dissent? Will TAI influence the economics of state surveillance practices and civil liberties? Understanding these dynamics will help policymakers harness TAI’s benefits while mitigating its political risks.

Relatedly, TAI will likely transform both individual and collective intelligence in ways that require economic analysis. Research is needed on how AI affects information markets and knowledge production. These questions connect to foundational economic concepts of information asymmetry, public goods, and knowledge spillovers.

AI safety and alignment.  AI safety and alignment refer to the challenge of ensuring AI systems behave consistently with human values and intentions.7 As AI grows more powerful and autonomous, the economic implications of their safety and alignment become crucial. How do the costs of AI safety and alignment compare to the economic benefits? What are the economic incentives for developing safe and aligned AI systems? And with whom should they be aligned?

Economists can develop frameworks and methodologies to align AI systems with social preferences and welfare.23 We have experience designing mechanisms for harmonizing the interests of agents with their principals. How can social welfare functions be adapted to capture the complexities of AI alignment? What economic mechanisms can be designed to internalize the positive and negative externalities generated by AI systems? How can we design incentive structures that encourage developers and users to prioritize alignment with broader societal goals? How can market mechanisms promote the development of safe and aligned AI systems? What tools can address the challenges of preference aggregation and value learning in AI systems?

One question concerns the trade-off between growth and safety.18 TAI systems may significantly increase economic growth but also affect the potential for catastrophic and even existential risks to humanity. What methods can economists develop to assess potential existential risks from TAI? If TAI also mitigates other risks or extends longevity, then how can we assess the trade-offs? Under what conditions is it rational to continue rapid AI progress or to slow or halt it?

An important factor to consider is the risk of AI race dynamics, whereby actors who benefit from being the first to develop higher capabilities prioritize speed over safety. For example, within labs, individual researchers may perceive career benefits to advancing more rapidly. Within nations, labs may race against each other to be the first to ship more powerful capabilities. And at the geopolitical scale, individual countries may race to outdo each other. In a worst-case scenario, race dynamics create existential risks. This is a classic externality problem, and economists have experience both in analyzing externalities and designing measures to internalize them. Another relevant question is how to address the tension between the economic benefits and the safety risks of open source systems.

Meaning and well-being.  Keynes’ prediction about solving the “economic problem” raises fundamental questions about human purpose and fulfillment in a TAI world.20 What can economics contribute to our understanding of meaning and well-being in a world without work? How can we analyze the production and distribution of non-monetary sources of fulfillment? Importantly, what is our ultimate objective in a world where machines can perform essentially all work? Is it desirable for work to maintain its current societal importance if we achieve TAI?

The psychological and social impacts of widespread labor displacement may present a complex challenge. Interestingly, some studies show that retirees experience increased happiness and life satisfaction, while the involuntarily unemployed tend to suffer decreased well-being. This raises several questions: What factors contribute to the positive experience of retirees versus the negative experience of the unemployed? How do societal expectations, financial security, and the voluntary nature of retirement influence these outcomes? Can we design economic policies that mimic the positive aspects of retirement for those displaced by TAI?

Will individuals make welfare-maximizing choices on how to spend their time if labor market opportunities decline? Or are there some aspects of work that are subject to externalities or internalities and that justify policy interventions to encourage work even if its economic value declines?24 For example, externalities may arise when an individual’s work affects others in society beyond just producing marketable output, such as by fostering social connections or political stability. Internalities may occur when individuals do not fully internalize the effects of their work choices on their own welfare, such as effects on mental health and loneliness. In hindsight, it would have been useful to measure mental health in teens before, during, and after social media were introduced with a keener eye. How can we accurately measure and model these externalities and internalities? What policy interventions might be justified to address these market failures, and how would they differ from current labor market policies?

As we potentially transition to a post-work society, economics will play a crucial role in shaping new institutions to support human flourishing. What frameworks can help us analyze what provides meaning when TAI can handle most economic tasks? How might the distribution of meaning-generating activities be optimized for social welfare? Can TAI itself help create or facilitate new sources of meaning and fulfillment? How can we equitably distribute the benefits of TAI, not just in terms of material wealth, but also in terms of access to fulfilling activities and meaning?

Transition dynamics.  Optimizing policies and institutions for a world of TAI is not enough. We must also successfully navigate the transition from our current economic institutions, organizations, and processes. As technology advances, bottlenecks are likely to emerge. Furthermore, some complementary factors (e.g. human skills, organizational structures, regulatory frameworks) will remain fixed in the short term and only adjust over time. The success of the transition will depend in large part on identifying and managing these bottlenecks and complementary factors.

Transitional dynamics deserve particular attention as the speed of adjustment following TAI could determine the effects on labor markets, including the prevalence of technological unemployment. The mismatch between rapidly evolving AI capabilities and slower-moving complementary factors could create significant adjustment costs. In addition, how do policy interventions—such as targeted retraining subsidies, adaptive regulatory sandboxes, and organizational-innovation grants—differentially accelerate the adaptation of complementary factors and thereby minimize aggregate adjustment costs during the rollout of TAI? There are many pathways from our current pre-TAI equilibrium to the new post-TAI economy. Research that informs policy during this transition phase could significantly enhance social welfare.

Methodologies for the Economics of TAI

Economics provides a rich toolkit to analyze social-science questions. Moreover, TAI may itself create new tools for economists. We lay out the main methodologies we envision to make progress on the TAI research agenda outlined above.

Theoretical approaches.  Economic theory plays a crucial role in understanding the potential economic impacts of TAI. Since TAI may represent a radical break from the past, one of the primary difficulties faced by empirical researchers is the scarcity of relevant historical data to extrapolate from. A significant amount of work in this field involves predicting a highly uncertain future. In this context, theoretical approaches that leverage higher-level regularities from the past—such as fundamental laws of economics—become especially valuable.

These approaches encompass a range of modeling techniques to understand economic shifts. Growth models, including those focusing on AI take-off dynamics, are at the forefront of this research. These models aim to capture non-linear and potentially explosive growth patterns that TAI might induce, helping to forecast scenarios of rapid technological advancement and its economic consequences. Complementing these are micro-to-macro approaches that bridge the gap between individual-level impacts of AI adoption and their aggregate effects on the broader economy.

A special focus within theoretical approaches is on normative frameworks, particularly those drawing from welfare theorems, social choice, and public finance principles. These frameworks address critical questions about the societal implications of TAI, such as how to equitably share the benefits and how to reform taxation systems in a world where traditional labor may be significantly diminished. How can AI development be steered in socially beneficial directions?8,26 By tackling these normative questions, theoretical approaches not only help predict the future economic landscape but also provide valuable insights for policymakers and society at large in navigating the transformative effects of AI.

A transformative AI dashboard.  Extensive work is already underway to track current AI capabilities directly (see e.g., HAI’s AI Index Report 202429). Economic indicators of a coming AI-driven boom in economic growth are less developed but would also be valuable because the relationships between benchmark task scores and economic impacts are not always intuitive or deterministic. Nordhaus takes a first step in this direction, looking for signs that computing is substituting for labor well enough to drive a near-term growth explosion.32 As of the date of his work, he largely does not find them. But the evidence may change as TAI comes closer and as other metrics are examined.

Analysis on this topic could extend to many other economic indicators, such as the substitution of labor for capital across various links in the AI and robotics supply chains. Further insights could arise by studying trends in a broader range of measures of substitutability: for example, the elasticity of substitution among different types of labor and capital instead of their aggregates. This data could fit a variety of growth models, reflecting differing assumptions about hard-to-measure variables, such as the relationship between research breakthroughs and economic growth on a given time horizon. Finally, by keeping the associated data and model-based forecasts current with an easily accessible “economic transformation dashboard,” researchers and policymakers could stay up to date about whether a period of AI-driven explosive growth appears to be approaching, and if so, what shape it is taking, as described in further depth in the online appendix.

New metrics for welfare.  New metrics are also needed for assessing economic welfare and consumption. As AI and other digital technologies become responsible for a larger share of production and distribution, the marginal costs of many goods and services will fall to nearly zero. When goods have zero price, they often have zero weight in GDP as it is conventionally measured. Likewise, labor productivity is typically measured as GDP per hour worked, so any mismeasurement of GDP will ripple through to productivity measures as well.

New methods, such as massive online choice experiments, can help assess the valuations that consumers have for goods and services that are poorly captured by traditional measures.10 As these methods are extended, refined, and scaled, they can create an updated measurement toolkit to better track AI’s contributions in the coming years.

Task-level assessments of potential impact.  It has proven fruitful to analyze the effects of AI and related technologies at the task level rather than the level of entire occupations, firms, or industries. This method has been applied to understand the potential effects of machine learning and generative AI on work and employment.11,12,15 While prior work used the U.S. Department of Labor’s O*Net taxonomy of about 18,000 tasks, future work could apply natural language processing to classify hundreds of millions of job postings and résumés, creating a much more fine-grained and dynamic task taxonomy.

Simulating economies using AI agents.  A fascinating new approach in economic research leverages AI itself, particularly through simulations and agent-based modeling. By creating LLM-based agents, researchers can simulate human behavior with increasing accuracy and at scale.16 Imagine the potential of modeling thousands, even millions, of these agents interacting in a simulated economy. The simulations could potentially produce similar outputs to randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to assess alternative policy options and interventions but at much greater speed. This may offer new insights into the economy and how AI might reshape labor, consumer behavior, industrial growth, and unforeseen economic bottlenecks.

Simulations are also increasingly used to develop AI systems, especially for robotics. What are the economic implications of developing simulation-based AI systems? What are the externalities associated with simulations and thus the welfare implications of creating these as a public good (e.g., open source) or establishing interoperability standards? How do the costs and benefits of using simulations to train AI compare with traditional data collection methods, particularly in industries with high physical-world uncertainty? What investment strategies best reduce the reality gap and improve real-world robot performance? How will early adopters gain competitive advantages, and what risks will late adopters face if simulation technologies remain imperfect?

Scenario planning.  Scenario planning offers a structured approach to preparing for multiple possible futures in the context of TAI. Unlike forecasting, which typically attempts to predict the most likely future state, scenario planning develops a set of distinct but plausible futures to help researchers and organizations understand different possible outcomes.21

This methodology is particularly valuable for studying TAI given the high degree of uncertainty around both the development timeline and the eventual capabilities. By systematically exploring different combinations of key variables—such as the speed of AI development, the degree of AI capabilities, the distribution of productivity gains, and the evolution of labor markets—researchers can identify robust economic patterns and outcomes.

The scenario-planning process can be enhanced by incorporating insights from other methodological approaches discussed earlier in this article. Theoretical models can help define the parameters and relationships that shape different scenarios, while simulations can test the internal consistency of various narratives. This integrated approach helps identify critical indicators and economic mechanisms across multiple scenarios. Moreover, scenario planning bridges technical, economic research, and policy communities, as well as the broader public, through a common framework for analyzing TAI futures.

Conclusion

The transition to an economy shaped by TAI will not follow a predetermined path. Some scenarios offer the promise of vastly enhanced wealth, where TAI drives unprecedented productivity, improves social welfare, and distributes benefits fairly. However, without thoughtful management, the outcome could be dystopian, with increased inequality, mass unemployment, social instability, and even catastrophe, leaving many people worse off.

This research agenda highlights the key questions and encourages researchers to develop the tools necessary to shape policies that maximize positive outcomes. By identifying key economic indicators, anticipating challenges, and advancing this research agenda, we hope to increase the likelihood that TAI will lead to shared prosperity and a sustainable future for humanity.

As the research agenda outlined in this article progresses, it will naturally give rise to important insights that are relevant for economic policymakers. Key areas may include:

  • Reforming labor laws to account for changes in employment

  • Adapting taxation systems to ensure fair distribution

  • Revamping education and skill development programs

  • Strengthening social insurance and income-distribution mechanisms

  • Maintaining social and political stability in the face of rapid technological change

  • Adjusting macroeconomic policy frameworks

  • Updating antitrust and market regulations

  • Refining intellectual property frameworks to balance innovation incentives with societal benefits

  • Developing environmental and resource policies

  • Establishing global TAI governance structures to ensure responsible development and deployment

By addressing these policy areas proactively, we can work toward harnessing the full potential of TAI while mitigating its risks and ensuring its benefits are broadly shared across society.

There is a critical need for interdisciplinary research that integrates economics, computer science, public policy, and other social sciences. While significant resources are being allocated to the technical development of TAI, there has been comparatively little investment in understanding its economic implications and preparing policies to steer TAI in desirable directions and prepare for the impacts.

Immediate action is essential. The necessary next steps include articulating a more comprehensive research agenda, establishing working groups, striking partnerships across sectors, and securing institutional support for these research efforts. A proactive approach will be crucial to ensure TAI enhances human welfare rather than exacerbating existing inequalities.

Preparing for TAI requires robust policy frameworks to manage disruptions and shape outcomes aligned with societal goals. Given the relatively slow rate at which organizations and processes change, investments in understanding the economics of TAI cannot afford to wait until powerful technology is created. With timely attention, we can seize the opportunities TAI offers while shaping its direction and mitigating its risks, in service of a future of broadly shared prosperity and human flourishing.
