item.title: Agency as a New Organizing Abstraction for Computer Science
item.dc:creator: Ian Foster
item.description: Considering agency is a candidate for organizing abstraction for structuring and reasoning about autonomous computational systems.
item.content:encoded:
The recent surge of interest in AI has been driven largely by advances in machine learning models, particularly large neural networks trained on massive datasets. These models have achieved striking capabilities in perception, language, and pattern recognition, reshaping both research and practice.

At the same time, an increasing number of deployed AI systems are no longer best understood as isolated inference engines. Instead, they take the form of agents: computational entities that persist over time, initiate actions, pursue goals, and interact continuously with their environments. Classical AI research has long defined agents as entities that perceive and act within an environment,5 and multiagent systems research has explored autonomy and interaction for decades.9 What is new is not the conceptual notion of an agent, but its operational realization under conditions that stress existing abstractions in specific, identifiable ways.

Recent systems demonstrate that language models can autonomously select and invoke external APIs, transforming stateless inference engines into systems that take consequential actions.7 Multiagent frameworks enable AI agents to collaborate on complex tasks through extended conversations, persisting state across interactions that may span hours. Agents that interleave reasoning and action can execute multi-step workflows, invoking computational tools and interpreting results without step-by-step human guidance.10

This transition exposes limitations in existing abstractions—not merely a new application layer, but a reorganization of computation that challenges foundational assumptions across operating systems, programming languages, verification, and human-computer interaction.

Taken together, these observations motivate treating agency not merely as an application-level concern, but as a candidate organizing abstraction for structuring and reasoning about autonomous computational systems. Framing systems in terms of agency reveals these challenges as structural rather than isolated engineering difficulties. Agentic AI also raises profound questions of governance, accountability, and social impact.1 This Opinion column focuses on technical challenges amenable to computer science research; we do not claim that better abstractions alone will resolve questions of values and policy.

What Makes a System Agentic?

I use the term agency to denote an abstraction over persistent computational entities that maintain internal state, pursue goals, initiate actions, and interact continuously with their environment and with humans over time. Four properties, taken together, characterize agentic operation.

Agentic systems are persistent, operating over extended periods and accumulating state, context, and experience. Unlike stateless services or batch jobs, they maintain continuity that influences future behavior. This persistence complicates resource management, failure handling, and reasoning about long-term effects, particularly when systems must be upgraded or audited while in operation.

Agentic systems are autonomous. They decide when to act rather than responding solely to external requests. This autonomy, though partial and constrained, fundamentally shifts computation from reactive to proactive.

Agentic systems are goal-directed. Their behavior is shaped by objectives that may require planning, monitoring, adaptation, and revision over time. Goals are often underspecified or conflicting, forcing agents to make trade-offs rather than execute fixed procedures.

Finally, agentic systems operate in open environments, interacting with APIs, tools, physical instruments, humans, and other agents in settings that cannot be fully specified in advance. Their actions are frequently consequential, consuming real resources and producing effects that may be difficult or impossible to undo.

Individually, none of these properties is new. What distinguishes contemporary agentic systems is the combination of all four properties, enabled by foundation models that support flexible behavior across diverse domains. This combination creates operational challenges that existing abstractions address only partially.

Where Current Abstractions Fall Short

Deployments of agentic systems expose a set of recurring failure modes that are not well addressed by existing computational abstractions.

One class of failure arises because agentic systems generate behavior dynamically rather than executing predefined procedures. Traditional systems expose fixed APIs and can be validated against their specified interfaces. Agentic systems respond to natural language inputs that are imprecise and essentially unbounded, pursuing goals through dynamically constructed action sequences that cannot be fully anticipated at design time. Consider an agent tasked with monitoring a cloud deployment. When it detects an anomaly, it may autonomously provision resources, invoke diagnostic tools, or roll back changes. Current container and process abstractions assume externally defined resource bounds. An agent that autonomously spawns subprocesses, allocates memory, or invokes paid APIs can exceed budgets in ways that become visible only after significant cost has been incurred. Agentic systems require proactive constraint enforcement that can anticipate and prevent costly actions before they occur.

A second difficulty concerns life-cycle management, as agentic systems do not fit cleanly into existing notions of process startup, execution, and termination. Batch jobs terminate. Services respond to requests and return to idle states. Agentic systems blur these boundaries. An agent may be “running” in the sense of maintaining state and awaiting opportunities to act, without actively consuming cycles. It may spawn child agents that outlive their parent, each pursuing independent goals with its own accumulated context—unlike forked processes that inherit fixed execution state. It may accumulate context that makes termination costly in terms of lost learning. When should such a system be terminated? How should its accumulated state be preserved or transferred? Current process models provide no principled answers.

Failure attribution becomes more complex when autonomous systems make decisions through extended sequences of reasoning and action rather than through isolated function calls. When a traditional program fails, debugging typically involves identifying a specific function call, assertion, or resource exhaustion. When an agentic system fails, the cause may be distributed across a sequence of locally reasonable decisions that compound into globally undesirable outcomes. Unlike classical planners that offer soundness guarantees, LLM-generated plans may be neither sound nor complete; exploration and refinement may incur significant cost or trigger irreversible state changes before errors become apparent. Agents that explicitly interleave reasoning and action over extended decision sequences exemplify this challenge, as errors may only become apparent after many intermediate steps have been executed.10 As in distributed systems, reconstructing such failures requires reasoning about partial orderings of events rather than linear execution traces, a challenge long recognized in classical work on distributed causality.4

A related mismatch appears at system interfaces, where long-standing assumptions about control flow and responsibility placement no longer hold. Microservices architectures assume request–response semantics, while workflow systems assume that control flow is known in advance. Both assumptions reflect an implicit placement of responsibility outside the computational component itself. Agentic systems shift responsibility inward, complicating classical end-to-end reasoning about where correctness, validation, and control should reside.6 Agent-initiated requests may violate implicit assumptions about rate, context, or intent that services designed for human users rely upon.

The accompanying table summarizes recurring failure modes observed in deployed agentic systems and the abstraction gaps they expose.

New Research Problems

These failure modes point to a set of concrete research problems that, when viewed through the lens of agency, present distinct challenges beyond questions of AI alignment or model capability development.

One challenge concerns execution environments for agentic systems, which must support launching, scheduling, pausing, and terminating agents while respecting persistent state and autonomous behavior. Key questions include how to express resource budgets for self-directed processes, what isolation guarantees apply when agents spawn agents, and how to detect problematic patterns before consequences become severe. These questions extend classical operating systems concerns into a new regime. The actor model2 provides relevant foundations through isolation and message passing, but was not designed for entities that maintain long-term goals and initiate actions based on accumulated experience rather than solely in response to incoming messages.

A second research direction concerns programming models capable of expressing constrained autonomy rather than fixed control flow. Agentic systems specified via goals and constraints rather than procedures challenge current paradigms. Key questions include how trade-offs between competing objectives should be expressed, how safety constraints can remain binding as agents adapt their strategies, and how the boundary between permitted and prohibited actions should be defined in environments that cannot be fully anticipated. Emerging frameworks for language model programming represent early steps toward higher-level abstractions, but comprehensive programming models for specifying and reasoning about constrained autonomous behavior remain underdeveloped.

Correctness becomes harder to define when system behavior adapts over time in response to partial information and evolving objectives. Verification for agentic systems cannot rely solely on classical notions of functional correctness or termination; instead, it may require probabilistic guarantees, regret bounds relative to optimal behavior, safety envelopes that bound worst-case outcomes, or temporal constraints on decision-making. Herbert Simon’s notion of bounded rationality8 provides useful conceptual grounding: agents operate under constraints of limited information, resources, and time, and correctness should be defined relative to those constraints. While long-horizon decision-making under uncertainty has been studied extensively, formal foundations for verifying constrained autonomous behavior remain limited.

Human oversight shifts from issuing commands to supervising ongoing behavior when agents operate continuously and at scale. Prior work on mixed-initiative systems3 highlights the difficulty of allocating control between humans and autonomous processes; these difficulties are magnified when agents operate persistently and at scale. Research questions include how oversight interfaces should convey agent decision making in interpretable terms, when agents should escalate decisions to human supervisors, and how limited human attention can be allocated effectively across populations of agents.

Implications for Computer Science

Historically, new computational phenomena have driven integration across subfields. The emergence of networking forced engagement between systems researchers, protocol designers, and application developers. The development of machine learning required collaboration between statisticians, optimization researchers, and domain experts.

Technical and governance challenges interact in important ways. Well-designed abstractions can make governance more tractable by providing hooks for auditing, constraint enforcement, and oversight. Poorly designed abstractions can make governance harder by obscuring behavior or creating fait accompli through deployed systems that resist modification. Technical researchers therefore have responsibilities extending beyond narrow efficiency metrics.

Agentic AI may play a similar integrative role. Addressing the challenges outlined above requires sustained interaction among traditionally distinct communities. Systems researchers must engage with intent and constraints; PL designers with uncertainty; theorists with bounded-agent correctness; HCI researchers with oversight at scale.

I do not claim that agentic AI necessarily demands a reorganization of computer science; that remains to be seen. Instead, I argue that specific, identifiable problems arising in agentic systems are poorly served by existing abstractions, and that addressing these problems presents concrete opportunities for productive research.

Conclusion

Agentic AI introduces operational challenges that stress existing computational abstractions in identifiable ways. Persistence, autonomy, goal-directedness, and open-world operation, combined through foundation model capabilities, create systems that current execution environments, programming models, and verification approaches handle imperfectly. Whether agency ultimately emerges as a durable organizing abstraction for computer science remains an open question, but current deployments of agentic systems already expose abstraction gaps that demand systematic attention. By engaging these technical problems directly, while maintaining appropriate humility about the distinct challenges of governance and social impact, computer science can contribute to a more principled understanding of autonomous computational systems.

item.title: The ‘Coloniality Problem’ in AI and the Call for ‘Decoloniality’
item.dc:creator: Damian Eke
item.description: Presenting a critical approach for computing professionals to ensure that AI serves humanity equitably rather than reinforce old power imbalances.
item.content:encoded:
The promises and risks of AI in healthcare, education, transportation, public service, finance, creative industries, security, and defense have extensively been highlighted in literature and practice.7 Issues such as algorithmic bias, data privacy and security, labor displacement, and lack of transparency have rightly gained significant attention in governance mechanisms. However, a deeper and more fundamental challenge persists largely unaddressed within mainstream technologies and in AI discourse and governance in particular: the ‘‘coloniality problem.” 

Coloniality, which is distinct from the historical and political process of colonialism, refers to the continued power imbalances that mirror colonial times of exploitation and control, epistemic hierarchies that neglects knowledge sources and systems from the Global South, as well as structural inequalities that persist long after formal decolonization.9,12 It is the persistence of colonial power relations embedded in knowledge production and development models that create dependencies8 that are often structurally produced through enduring economic, technological, and epistemic relations. In the context of computing, particularly in AI, this means that the very foundation of knowledge production, technological design, development and deployment often reproduces and exacerbates historical patterns of control and exploitation.11,14 There are obvious manifestations of inherent coloniality in the different stages of the AI innovation life cycle that are often captured as data colonialism,3 algorithmic colonialism,2 or simply AI colonialism.5 In this Opinion column, I argue that this is one problem computing professionals should care about. Ignoring it risks embedding biases and injustices into technologies that shape billions of lives in the Global Majority. I subsequently present decoloniality as a critical approach that can be used by computing professionals to address the coloniality problem; ensuring that AI serves humanity equitably rather than reinforcing old hierarchies and power imbalances under new digital forms.

AI and the Coloniality Problem

In a recent book chapter, Wakunuma et al.14 identified the different manifestations of coloniality in the AI innovation life cycle including in data, algorithms, mineral resources that inform AI infrastructure, AI governance and regulation, exploitation of labor for data labeling and in the lack of experts in AI development teams. From the data perspective, it is true that AI relies heavily on large-scale data extraction from populations who rarely control how it’s collected, used or monetized. This phenomenon is often referred to as “data colonialism’’ and involves the mining of data from the Global South for digital value under the guise of innovation or development, effectively commodifying human experience for the benefit of big technology corporations. An example here will be Facebook’s Free Basics which is a case that can be described as both data and digital colonialism.13 It was marketed as a free Internet service for developing markets aimed at bridging the digital divide by creating an ‘‘on ramp’’ to the Internet for millions of people. Introduced to many countries in Africa, Asia, and Latin America, this service ended up not meeting linguistic needs of target users, lacked local content, did not connect users to the global Internet but collected huge amounts of data from users as well as violating network neutrality principles.16 Users were only offered access to well curated websites selected by Facebook (as a gatekeeper) while their data—behavior, interests, communications—were harvested without appropriate benefits.

Algorithms that encode the biases found in data and often amplify them. Although the data often comes from the Global South, the power to design, train, and deploy algorithms is concentrated in a few countries in the Global North and Big Tech corporations. This means AI models are built using assumptions rooted in Western contexts and critically fail to capture diverse social realities, values and principles from the Global South. In such a case, there is a fundamental lack of awareness of colonial histories and power asymmetries, algorithms can perpetuate discrimination, marginalize minority languages and contexts, and give priority to certain values while erasing or neglecting others. This can often be reflected when AI-driven platforms developed for the Global South push Global North values and principles, undermining local cultures and knowledge systems.

Coloniality also manifests in algorithms that encode and often amplifies the biases found in data. AI is reliant on physical infrastructures powered by minerals like cobalt, lithium, and rare earth metals. These are often mined in many regions of the Global South under exploitative conditions that mirror colonial extraction. Local communities bear the environmental and social costs while profits flow elsewhere. This material dependency ties AI’s cutting-edge promise to extractive economies that sustain global inequalities. Related to this is the inexpensive and often hidden labor that sustains the AI life cycle where millions of workers in the Global South perform low-paid data labeling and content moderation for big tech companies. Like in the colonial times, these workers face precarious physical and psychological conditions, low wages, and little recognition in the AI value chain. This mirrors colonial patterns of extracting cheap labor.

Additionally, AI development teams often lack experts from underrepresented regions and communities in the Global South. This underpresentation has been highlighted by many scholars.1,15 This limits the contributions of perspectives, values and principles shaping how AI problems are defined and solved. Lack of diversity of the AI expert teams mean that systems are designed with blind spots on cultural contexts, local needs, and structural injustices reinforcing technological solutions that overlook or harm marginalized groups.

Finally, in the colonial times, colonial powers created legal systems for the colonized entities to serve their own economic and political interests whilst extracting resources, controlling lands, managing local labor, and suppressing resistance. Currently, AI governance mechanisms are currently being shaped by very powerful countries and corporations. Some governance efforts in the Global South are also mostly funded by Global North Actors and local voices and governance models are underrepresented. This reproduces a space that leaves little space for locally relevant accountability mechanisms or provisions that reflect the lived realities of those most affected by AI systems.

The Shortcomings of Current Responsible Innovation Approaches

In my years of experience, teaching undergraduate computer science students and doing research in interdisciplinary research groups in information systems, visibly progress has been made in the ethics of computing and AI education. This includes introducing computing professionals to responsible approaches such as responsible research and innovation, ethics-by-design as well impact assessment tools; to ensure that they create technologies that are ethical, lawful, socially acceptable, and fit for purpose as well as to avoid repeating mistakes that can cause real harm or reinforce injustice. These approaches vary in depth and structure and often focus on principles such as privacy, data protection, human rights and brother ethical considerations (e.g responsibility, accountability, safety, transparency, fairness, lack of discrimination, and trustworthiness) or societal outcomes like human well-being and inclusion. These focus points represent an emerging global consensus on responsible technology or AI design, development and deployment.6 The available approaches therefore provide a crucial ethical and legal vocabulary for responsible AI whilst laying its foundational framework. However, these approaches are conspicuously silent on the deep rooted issue of coloniality and its continued impact on contemporary technological innovations. This clear lack of focus on who defines AI risks, whose values are embedded in ethical frameworks, who is consistently excluded from shaping AI futures is characteristic of existing approaches. For example, when these approaches emphasize privacy and data protection, what is often missing is the inherent extractive nature of data practices in the Global South. The unbalanced flow of data where postcolonial populations and contexts are mined for training data without benefits or representation in model development constitutes a form of data and algorithmic colonialism that are rarely assessed via available evaluation criteria.

Moreso, existing approaches assume universal ethical standards without consideration for contextual epistemologies, cultural values, principles, needs and interests. Concepts like autonomy, fairness, privacy and trust are often defined in Western lens and there is little emphasis on relational concepts such as ubuntu and collective well-being and privacy that are common in postcolonial contexts. Often referred to as epistemic injustice, this neglect entrenches a near-monolithic review of ethics and governance of AI and other emerging technologies. This is a fundamental gap in theory, practice and education of responsible AI. Therefore, there is a need for computer professionals to confront these tendencies and legacies embedded in AI’s data, labor, infrastructure, epistemology, and ethics.

The Call for Decoloniality in AI Practice and Education

Given the identified gaps in existing responsible innovation approaches and impact assessments, decoloniality becomes an imperative as a response to the ‘coloniality problem’ in AI. As Wakunuma et al., opined, decoloniality is a critical element of trustworthy AI in postcolonial contexts and this means the ‘‘active process that seeks to address and dismantle the deep-seated impacts of coloniality on knowledge systems, technologies, cultures, identities, and social structures.’’14 This is not a rejection of technology, but a call to reimagine its purposes, architectures, and epistemologies.10 It involves building and shaping technologies that are culturally relevant and sensitive, locally governed and ecologically sustainable. This call is for both practice and education.

In education, this involves embedding decoloniality into curricula where students are taught to recognize historical and structural injustices in tech, going beyond existing Western theories to social theories, history and global perspectives. It also means the use of diverse use cases and the promotion of multilingual, culturally relevant examples. Decoloniality also involves ensuring that students understand the meaning and impact of power imbalances in the innovation life cycle.

In practice, decoloniality entails active involvement of local communities in defining interests, problems and co-creating solutions as well as the rejection of extractive approaches in data and mineral resources. It also involves the support for open data infrastructures that ensures local ownership; building collaborations where local experts are co-leads, recognizing and acknowledging local contributions. Most importantly, conduct decoloniality impact assessment4 to identify colonial biases and harmful assumptions.

I therefore call for the explicit recognition of the coloniality problem and the need for decoloniality within the ACM Code of Ethics and professional conduct, including clear guidance on how AI systems may reproduce historical power asymmetries through data, design assumptions, evaluation benchmarks, and deployment contexts. This type of recognition will provide visibility to a form of harm that is currently underspecified, despite its pervasive impact on AI design and use globally. Mitigating the coloniality problem requires concrete professional practices. This approach requires; participatory design led by impacted communities, data governance that identifies gaps in representation, impact assessments centered on geopolitical power structures and accountability that moves from “token diversity” to a genuine redistribution of authority.

Conclusion

I argue that this call to engage with decoloniality is not and should not be simply an act of academic curiosity. It is a matter of professional responsibility and ethical obligation. The ACM Code of Ethics emphasizes the importance of avoiding harm, ensuring fairness, and respecting the dignity of all people. The coloniality problem described above reproduces harm, unfairness and discrimination to populations in the Global Majority. That means decoloniality is essential to fulfilling ACM’s ethical commitments. Crucially, the commitment to decoloniality requires interdisciplinary collaboration between computer professionals, ethicists, legal experts, local communities in Global South and North. It requires humility and reflexivity and the willingness to embrace a pluriversal approach that recognizes the critical importance of values, interests, beliefs and contexts in different parts of the world. In the current ecosystem marked by renewed attacks on diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI), embedding decolonial responsibility within the ACM Code of Ethics and Professional conduct would represent a decisive step toward a more just, accountable, and globally legitimate AI profession.

item.title: What Voice and AI Change About My Writing
item.dc:creator: Morissa Schwartz
item.description: On using voice tools to get words onto a page, and AI tools to help arrange and develop them.
item.content:encoded:
At 12, I used speech recognition to write a report about reptiles. The software needed considerable supervision, including repeated attempts to get the word “reptile” right. Dictation took longer than typing. I kept using it because writing and typing hurt, and speaking made the work less painful. That experience still shapes how I think about writing tools. If someone had measured only how quickly I finished the report, they would have missed why I was using the software.

Today, I have arthritis, and voice input remains part of how I write. I also use an AI assistant I call Penny. I speak ideas into my phone, sometimes adding a point after I have already moved on to another thought. Penny can group those thoughts and suggest an order. That gives me text to work with without having to type every word. Then I read it, question it, and revise. The point I am trying to make still needs my attention, even when the sentences are already there.

Speech recognition and generative AI ask different things of me as a writer. With dictation, I need to check whether the text captures what I said. When AI helps organize or draft, I also need to examine what it has done to the argument. Choosing which idea comes first can change what everything after it seems to mean. An omitted detail can change what a reader understands. I can welcome help with the draft while still needing to decide whether the result says what I intended.

While I was developing a talk about AI, Penny edited out a reference to Isaac Asimov. I put it back. I have a doctorate in literature; Asimov belonged in the talk I wanted to give. That small revision is a useful example of what remains my work. A proposed edit needs to serve the purpose of the piece. In this case, the reference connected the subject to the literature that informs how I think about it. The software could suggest removing it. I had to decide whether that made the talk better.

I also have to notice when a sentence claims more than I mean. “This helped me” and “this helps writers” make different promises to a reader. The first can describe my experience. The second asks for evidence beyond it. A polished sentence can make that shift easy to overlook. If I generalize from my experience, I owe the reader an explanation of what supports that broader claim. My experience gives me something to contribute to a discussion about access and authorship, with limits on what I can conclude about anyone else’s work.

There is a practical responsibility here for anyone whose name goes on the work. ACM’s Policy on Authorship places responsibility for content with human authors. I need to know which statements describe my experience, which depend on outside sources, and which express my judgment. When I rely on a source, I need to check that it supports the claim. I used OpenAI Codex in developing the pitch and synopsis for this post, and its help is disclosed below. Explaining that process lets an editor understand how the text came together and ask informed questions about it.

My experience also makes me want organizations to ask more precise questions about writing tools. What part of the work is the tool helping with? What information will it receive? What will a person need to review? Those are practical reflections from my own writing, rather than a tested policy framework or an account of administering workplace accommodations. Different input methods can coexist with expectations about accuracy, confidentiality, and editorial judgment. I would like an assessment of my work to account for both the quality of the result and the physical effort required to produce it.

That is why speed alone tells me too little. Dictation was useful to me even when it was slower. AI assistance adds another consideration: I have to leave room for the reading and revision the draft requires. Producing more text does not by itself tell me whether I have communicated well. For my own writing, I want to be able to explain why a passage belongs, what supports it, and what I hope a reader will understand.

I began using voice tools because getting words onto a page could hurt. I now use tools that can also help arrange and develop those words. They change the process, and I value that help. The responsibility that comes with my name remains: to decide what I mean, recognize when the draft has moved away from it, and make the changes I can stand behind.

Disclosure: OpenAI Codex helped organize, draft, and revise this post, including its pitch and synopsis.

Morissa Schwartz is a Forbes 30 Under 30 honoree in Media and founder of GenZ Publishing. She holds a doctorate in literature and writes about AI, accessibility, work, and human judgment.

item.title: How Immigration and Federal Funding Sustain American AI Leadership
item.dc:creator: Nur Ahmed
item.description: America's AI leadership rests on a foundation of international scientific talent and federal research funding.
item.content:encoded:
America’s competitive advantage in AI appears to be driven by the scale and agility of its private sector. Leading technology companies develop the most advanced models, control most computational resources, and hire a large share of new AI Ph.D.s.1 These firms have invested hundreds of billions of dollars in infrastructure, far exceeding public spending.35 This resource consolidation creates the appearance of a fully self-sustaining industry. However, the commercial success of generative AI builds directly on decades of federally funded academic research, and the talent pipeline supplying both industry and academia remains deeply dependent on public investment.33

Key Insights

  • America’s AI leadership is widely attributed to private capital and compute scale. In fact, two public goods underpin it: international scientific talent and federal research funding. Startups built on both account for more than $1.6 trillion in valuation, more than all other combinations combined.

  • Federal funding and industry R&D are complements. AI patents that cite both federally funded and industry-funded science have roughly twice the median commercial value of patents drawing on either source alone, indicating that public investment amplifies private returns rather than crowding them out.

  • Proposed immigration restrictions and science budget cuts of 40–57% directly threaten the inputs that produced U.S. AI leadership. Sustaining competitiveness requires expanding visa pathways for AI-relevant talent and reinforcing federal research investment.

Our analysis uses unique hand-collected data tracing individuals from doctoral training through patent creation to startup formation. We find that commercial success in AI depends on two factors: international scientific talent and sustained federal research investment. The private sector scales innovations that first emerged from publicly funded training programs and basic research. This pattern echoes the Manhattan Project and Apollo programs, where government expenditure and émigré scientists such as Enrico Fermi and John von Neumann enabled American technological leadership.8

Private firms systematically underinvest in basic research because fundamental discoveries are difficult to patent and their value diffuses broadly, making it difficult for any single firm to capture returns.23 Since the 1950s, federal agencies have addressed this market failure by underwriting high-risk, long-term inquiry that ultimately drives significant commercial value.10–12,14,25 Using novel datasets covering doctoral graduations, patent citations, and startup formation, we demonstrate that this pattern has intensified in AI.

We show that international researchers now constitute the majority of the advanced AI research workforce and are disproportionately represented in both academic recognition and commercial value creation. Their contributions appear not only in doctoral enrollment statistics but also in conference award data spanning five premier AI venues, in authorship of the most-cited AI papers, and in the founding teams of the highest-valued private AI companies. Our data shows that immigrant founders are present in firms accounting for more than 95% of the aggregate valuation among the most promising private AI companies.

Federal research funding forms the second pillar supporting this talent ecosystem. Approximately 75–80% of computer science (CS) doctoral students receive federal support during training, enabling the high-risk fundamental research that underlies commercial AI breakthroughs. Patents that cite both federally funded and industry-funded research have substantially higher commercial value than patents that rely on a single funding source. Startups founded by international researchers who received federal doctoral funding account for more than $1.6 trillion in valuation, underscoring the interdependence of these two inputs. Consequently, proposals to restrict high-skilled immigration2,24 or reduce federal science budgets22,30 directly threaten the key inputs that sustain U.S. competitiveness in AI. We quantify these contributions to show that sustaining U.S. competitiveness requires maintaining both reasonable immigration pathways and robust federal research funding.

International Researchers Drive American AI Excellence

International talent’s contribution to American innovation is well-documented across the technology sector. Immigrants have historically demonstrated higher rates of business formation than native-born individuals7,15 and are substantially overrepresented among founders of high-growth ventures, accounting for more than half of U.S. “unicorns” valued at more than $1 billion.3 In our study, we show that with AI, this pattern has not only persisted but intensified.

From Ph.D. programs to research excellence.  The composition of the U.S. AI research community has shifted markedly over the past two decades. Using data from the Computing Research Association (CRA) Taulbee Survey, we document that the share of international students earning Ph.D.s in CS in the U.S. increased from 45% in 2000 to 65.9% in 2024 (Figure 1).6 International Ph.D. recipients constitute a primary source of advanced AI research talent. The domestic doctoral pipeline, however, has not kept pace with demand, largely because the doctoral career track has failed to compete with industry careers for domestic CS undergraduates.32 Consequently, policies that make the U.S. less attractive to international graduate students in science and engineering could have significant adverse consequences for U.S. research capacity and technological competitiveness.

This dependence on international talent extends beyond doctoral enrollment. International representation is also pronounced in top-tier AI research recognition. Among Best Paper and Outstanding Paper award recipients at AAAI, ACL, CVPR, ICML, and NeurIPS from 2013 to 2024, we restrict our analysis to the 436 recipients affiliated with U.S.-based institutions. International researchers constitute an average of 61% of these U.S.-based awardees over the period. This share remains relatively stable despite substantial field growth and an increase in the number of awards granted annually, with the three-year moving average ranging between 54% and 68% throughout the sample period. These patterns indicate that international researchers account for a majority of award-recognized contributions across a broad set of AI subfields.

Author demographics of the 50 most-cited AI papers.  To better understand the relationship between researcher origin and institutional affiliation, we cross-tabulated these variables for the 205 unique authors of the 50 most-cited AI papers (see supplement, Figure A1) from the leading three AI conferences (AAAI, ICML, and NeurIPS). The results show that international researchers comprise 67.8% of this group (139 of 205). Within the subset of 158 authors at U.S. institutions, 93 (58.9%) are international, confirming that the majority of U.S.-based researchers producing top-tier AI scholarship were born and educated abroad. Taken together, these patterns indicate a distinct “brain gain,” in which the U.S. attracts a disproportionate share of the global AI talent pool.

From research to startup success.  This AI research talent directly generates commercial value. We examined the 2024 CB Insights AI 100 list to determine the origins of founders at the most promising U.S.-headquartered startups. Non-U.S. startups were excluded from all valuation analyses. Our analysis, updated through February 2026, indicates a significant disparity between startups with at least one international cofounder and those with exclusively U.S.-born founding teams.

As illustrated in Figure 2, startups with at least one international cofounder account for $1.71 trillion, or approximately 95% of the total valuation of companies with public valuations in our sample. In contrast, firms with exclusively U.S.-born founding teams account for just $81.25 billion. Excluding OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI, internationally founded startups still represent a valuation of $243.24 billion, approximately three times that of their U.S.-founded counterparts.

As a robustness check, we estimate founder valuation using a weighted allocation measure. Our baseline binary classification labels a startup as internationally founded if it has at least one non-U.S. cofounder. This assigns the full valuation of mixed teams to the international category and may overstate their aggregate contribution. To construct a more conservative measure, we distribute each startup’s valuation equally among its cofounders and aggregate by origin. Under this weighted allocation, international founders account for $999.68 billion (55.71%) and U.S. founders account for $794.82 billion (44.29%). This result confirms that international talent generates most of the total value in elite AI entrepreneurship even under a conservative allocation rule.

The equal-weight assumption obscures the outsized role that individual founders often play in shaping a startup’s direction. Apple had three cofounders, yet Steve Jobs, whose biological father was a Syrian immigrant, was widely regarded as the driving force of the firm. Empirical work by Choi et al.5 supports this intuition. Using premature founder deaths as a natural experiment, they found that the loss of a single founding team member causes large and persistent negative effects on firm performance over a 10-year period. Our weighted measure therefore likely understates the true economic contribution of individual international founders.

This dominance of international talent is consistent with prior research. More than 70% of immigrant founders at top U.S. AI startups first entered on student visas,13 indicating that U.S. universities serve as both recruitment and training pipelines for future AI entrepreneurs. The U.S. venture capital and compute ecosystem amplifies this talent pipeline, but functional upstream channels, including student visas and federal research grants, are necessary conditions for that ecosystem to access it.

From Federal Grants to Commercial AI

While private capital scales AI technologies, federal agencies have built the underlying research ecosystem since the 1950s. Agencies such as DARPA, the NSF, and the ONR have historically supported high-risk, long-term inquiry that the private sector, bound by shorter return horizons, could not justify.8 Here, we show that federal funding plays a major role in training the AI workforce, commercializing AI research through patents, and founding leading startups.

Underwriting doctoral education.  Federal agencies are the primary funding source for advanced AI research training in the U.S. Among computer science Ph.D. graduates from 2000 to 2019, 75–80% acknowledged U.S. federal agencies as their primary source of support.29 This persistent reliance shows how extensively federal grants support the doctoral infrastructure that trains the AI research workforce.

Funding sources of the 50 most-cited AI papers.  In our analysis of the 50 most-cited AI papers, a clear distinction emerges between funding sources based on institutional affiliation. Of these papers, 44% were U.S.-affiliated and federally funded, while 36% were U.S.-affiliated without such funding (see supplement, Figure A2). These findings confirm that federal funding remains a substantial driver of U.S.-based research output in AI.

From public research to private value.  Federal research investment generates measurable commercial returns. Using the Reliance on Science dataset19 merged with patent valuation data,16 we trace how federal funding influences the commercial value of U.S. patents granted by the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO).

The results suggest strong complementarities between public and private research funding. Among corporate AI patents that cite academic research, those that build on both federally funded and industry-funded science have median innovation values of $23.9 million in inflation-adjusted 1982 dollars. This figure is nearly double the $11 to $12 million median for patents that cite only federal or only industry research (Figure 3). This valuation gap indicates that the combination of public and private research inputs generates systematically higher economic returns than either alone.

The pattern holds across the entire distribution. Mean values reach $40.9 million (1982 dollars) for patents citing both funding sources compared to $33 to $39 million for single-source patents. These differences demonstrate that federal investment enables fundamental discoveries and amplifies the commercial value of industry research through complementary effects. Rather than crowding out private investment, federal funding reduces the risks of the ambitious, long-term research that industry typically avoids, allowing companies to build upon foundational public science. Federal research investment thus generates direct commercial returns while substantially amplifying private R&D effectiveness.

Our analysis indicates that federal funding during doctoral training is strongly associated with startup success. Among the elite AI startups in our sample, firms with at least one founder who received federal funding during doctoral or postdoctoral training account for $1.64 trillion in combined valuation, representing 91.4% of the total valuation (Figure 4). Conversely, companies without federally funded founders represent only 8.6% of the aggregate value (Figure 4). This valuation gap indicates that federally funded graduate programs produce founders uniquely equipped to build high-value AI companies.

The combined effect of international talent and federal training on startup value.  When international founder status and federal doctoral funding are examined together, the concentration of firm value becomes even more pronounced (Figure 5). Startups with at least one international founder and at least one founder who received federal funding during doctoral or postdoctoral training account for $1,636.71 billion in total valuation across 15 firms, a figure that exceeds the combined valuation of the remaining three quadrants.

Taken together, the evidence points to a continuous pipeline underpinning U.S. AI dominance. Public and private research converge to generate fundamental discoveries, which are then commercialized through patents and elite startups. Federal agencies underwrite most advanced AI training and basic research, with roughly three-quarters of U.S. CS Ph.D.s acknowledging federal support. Corporate laboratories contribute their own R&D, but the highest-value inventions emerge where corporate and federally supported research intersect. AI patents that cite research funded by both federal agencies and industry partners have roughly twice the median commercial value of patents drawing on federal-only or industry-only research. The same pattern appears on the entrepreneurial side. More than 90% of the aggregate valuation of leading AI startups traces to founders whose doctoral or postdoctoral work was federally funded. Our results suggest that American AI leadership emerges from the interaction between public research investment and private commercialization, rather than from either sector in isolation.

Potential Cost of Inaction

Despite their proven scientific and economic importance, both ingredients of U.S. AI leadership, international talent and federal research funding, currently face significant policy headwinds.

Decline of the U.S. AI talent pipeline.  Early 20th-century U.S. immigration restrictions produced a persistent decline in U.S. patenting and a relative gain for Canada.20 Recent evidence suggests that when the U.S. restricts high-skilled visas, multinational firms do not substitute with domestic workers but instead offshore affected positions and expand employment at foreign affiliates.9 The current environment presents comparable risks at a larger scale. The 93 international authors affiliated with U.S. institutions in the 50 most-cited AI papers (see supplement, Table A3) arrived through an immigration system whose continued openness cannot be taken for granted. The 15 startups in the upper-right quadrant of Figure 5, collectively valued at approximately $1.6 trillion, represent firms whose founding conditions required both immigration access and public research investment. Current immigration law, however, heavily favors large established corporations over startups and entrepreneurs in visa allocation,4 making high-growth firms most vulnerable to talent constraints.

Evidence of declining American competitive advantage has accumulated rapidly. In early 2025, U.S. scientists submitted 32% more job applications abroad,31 and 75% of postgraduate researchers reported considering leaving.36 These trends place at direct risk the populations our data identify as foundational to U.S. AI leadership: The 93 international researchers at U.S. institutions among the authors of the 50 most-cited AI papers, and the 15 startups at the intersection of international founding and federal doctoral training, collectively valued at more than $1.6 trillion. Survey data from researchers with papers at NeurIPS and ICML confirm that 69% of AI researchers residing in the U.S. identify visa and immigration problems as a significant impediment to conducting research,38 compared to 10–18% in Europe.2,24 One-third of departing Ph.D.s cite visa uncertainty as a key factor.2,24 Analysis of over 200 million scientific papers and surveys of more than 1,300 scientists document a steady, rapid increase in return migration from the U.S. to China, driven in significant part by the chilling effect of federal investigations and visa restrictions.37

Several governments have introduced policies designed to attract AI talent. For example, China now offers generous Ph.D. stipends and visa categories that do not require employer sponsorship.18 The National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence documented that Canada, the U.K., and China have each reformed their immigration systems with visa programs and stipends designed specifically to attract AI talent pushed away by U.S. bottlenecks.28 European institutions have begun explicit recruitment of U.S.-based scientists.17 The Global AI Talent Tracker reports that 28% of top-tier AI researchers were working in China in 2022, up from 11% in 2019.26

Contraction of federal research investment.  The other input in this pipeline, federal research funding, is also contracting. As shown in Figure 3, the highest-value AI patents depend on a public research base that federal cuts would eliminate, reducing returns to private R&D in the process. Recent work33,34 suggests that stagnant federal funding relative to industry compensation is eroding the viability of academic AI careers and may reduce CS enrollment. In addition to these budgetary constraints, 45% of U.S.-based scientists of Chinese descent who currently hold federal grants now wish to avoid applying for future funding out of fear of federal government prosecution.37

The U.S. faces proposed cuts of roughly 40% to the NIH and 57% to the NSF,30 compounding recent budget declines.22 These agencies fund the doctoral training infrastructure that produced the founders of firms now valued at $1.64 trillion (Figure 4). While China increased R&D expenditure by 8.3% in 2024,21 the gap in public research investment is widening. The 75–80% federal funding rate among CS Ph.D. graduates reflects how thoroughly the U.S. research workforce depends on public investment at the training stage. Reducing that funding would weaken the connection between public investment and private value creation that our patent and startup data documents.12

Policy Recommendations

To sustain American leadership in AI, policies need to reinforce the ecosystem that produced it. Here are three policy recommendations that address recent restrictions on immigration and federal funding.

Expand visa allocations for AI-relevant occupations.  Numerical caps on skilled-worker visas have remained static while demand for AI talent has grown substantially. International researchers at U.S. institutions who authored award-winning papers or the 50 most-cited AI papers are the population most directly affected by these caps. Survey data indicates that 69% of U.S.-based AI researchers view visa issues as serious obstacles, a rate three to seven times higher than in European countries.38 Our analysis does not include visa issuance data or cap utilization rates, but the magnitude of this disparity suggests that current allocations materially constrain the AI talent pool. Moreover, firm-level evidence demonstrates that multinational companies respond to H-1B rejections by expanding employment at foreign affiliates, particularly in China, India, and Canada, with the most globally established firms replacing nearly one-for-one each lost visa with an overseas hire.9 Rigid visa caps therefore restrict the domestic supply of specialized talent and inadvertently shift AI-related employment and innovation to competing nations.

Create simpler pathways to residency.  International researchers constitute 66% of new CS Ph.D. recipients (Figure 1), and more than 70% of immigrant founders at leading AI startups first entered the U.S. on student visas.13 The current system requires these graduates to enter a lottery-based process with no guaranteed path to permanent residency,27 creating uncertainty that Roach and Skrentny27 show depresses entrepreneurial entry among international STEM Ph.D.s. Implementing a direct route from STEM Ph.D. completion to permanent residency would improve the retention of specialized talent already developed by U.S. institutions. Although the U.S. currently trains the majority of international AI researchers, a substantial share of them cite the restrictive U.S. immigration system as their primary reason for leaving.3,26

Sustain and strengthen federal research investment.  Private markets systematically underinvest in long-horizon, foundational research, making expanded federal funding necessary to correct this market failure and preserve the knowledge base that enables future breakthroughs. Federal agencies fund 75–80% of CS doctoral training (Figure 3), and AI patents citing both federal and industry research exhibit median commercial values nearly double those citing a single source. Startups whose founders received federal support account for 91.4% of elite AI startup valuation. Proposed cuts of 40–57% to major science agencies30 would reduce the training pipeline and basic research infrastructure that our data identifies as key ingredients of commercial AI success.

Conclusion

Our results challenge the prevailing view that U.S. AI leadership is primarily a function of the capital resources and computing scale of its leading firms. We find that this leadership rests on a foundation of global talent drawn to U.S. universities and sustained by federal research investment. Restrictions on high-skilled immigration or cuts to public research funding would weaken that foundation directly.

item.title: A New Era for Inside Risks
item.dc:creator: Nancy Leveson
item.description: We need creative new approaches to safety and security problems and perhaps entirely new ways of tackling them.
item.content:encoded:
Peter Neumann, who created the Communications Inside Risks column, passed away in May 2026. The Communications Inside Risks columns were initially monthly one-page columns on the last page of each monthly issue. After June 2008, the last-page columns evolved into longer multipage Inside Risks columns appearing several times yearly in the front pages of the magazine.

I have been asked to take over the editorial duties of this column, and I am honored to do so. For those who do not know me, my Ph.D. was in computer science, and I have worked on safety, and to a lesser extent security, for more than 40 years in both industry and academia.

During his long tenure, Peter was assisted by the ACM Committee on Computers and Public Policy (CCPP), which he chaired. When ACM disbanded the CCPP, Peter retained its members as an editorial advisory group. The panel consisted of: Steve Bellovin, Peter Denning, Virgil Gligor, Nancy Leveson, Dave Parnas, Jerry Saltzer, Lauren Weinstein, Jim Horning (until January 2013), and more recently Kevin Fu, Ben Zorn, and Zeynep Tufekci. Col. William (“Dollar”) Young (ret.) recently joined. I will continue to rely on the members of the Inside Risks editorial panel for ideas, initial editing, and reviews for Communications Opinion columns. I also invite your reader suggestions for potential topics to be covered (leveson@mit.edu). The future of the ACM Risks Forum is being handled by a different group (see https://www.acm.org/about-acm/risks-forum).

Philosophical Foundations

Peter is greatly missed by those who knew him or read his papers and Inside Risks columns. He conceived of this column as an online dialogue on risks to the public involving such issues as safety, privacy, ethics, and legal responsibility. I will continue the column spirit unchanged, particularly Peter’s emphasis on a total systems approach to tackling computer-related risks.

While always a fan of simplicity, Peter understood that things can be inherently complex. In memoriam to Peter, Steve Bellovin wrote: “The real trick, and one fiendishly difficult to pull off, is to eliminate the unnecessary complexity. But you can’t eliminate complexity by changing one part of a system, because they all interact. [Peter] understood that, both the problem of complexity and the difficulty in eliminating it. Too few people do.”

In 2000, Peter reflected on what had happened during the first ten years of the Inside Risks column: “Our basic conclusions have not changed much over the years—despite many advances in the technology. Indeed, this lack of change itself seems like a serious risk. Overall, the potential risks have monotonously if not monotonically become worse, relative to increased system/network vulnerabilities and increased threats, and their consequent domestic and worldwide social implications with respect to national stability, e-commerce, personal well-being, and many other factors.”a

The challenges that Peter wrote approximately 26 years ago have not diminished. He wrote further: “Enormous advances in computing power have diversely challenged our abilities to use information technology intelligently. Distributed systems and the Internet have opened up new possibilities. Security, reliability, and predictability remain seriously inadequate. Privacy, safety, and other socially significant attributes have suffered. Risks have increased in part because of greater complexity, worldwide connectivity, and dependence on systems and people of unknown trustworthiness; vastly many more people are now relying on computers and the Internet; neophytes are diminishing the median level of risk awareness. The mass-market software marketplace eagerly creates new functionality, but is not sufficiently responsive to the needs of critical applications. The development process is often unmanageable for complex systems, which tend to be late, over budget, noncompliant, and in some cases cancelled altogether. Much greater discipline is needed. Many efforts seek quick-and-dirty solutions to complex problems, and long-time readers of this column realize how counterproductive that can be in the long run.”

Indeed, the advances in computing technology and use have created even greater potential risks and few effective solutions. The new problems being created seem to be greatly outpacing our solutions for them. As a profession, we are responsible for the impact, both positive and negative, of our technology on the world.

We still need creative new approaches to safety and security problems and perhaps entirely new ways of tackling them. Incremental improvements in the current solutions are not keeping up with the increasing challenges. There is no shortage of new risks posed by the rapidly changing technology and its new applications.

Some Important Future Risk Concerns

What are some of the topics we should be working on and encouraging our students to pursue? Many of the previous security-related concerns continue such as:

  • Rampant increases of identity theft, ransomware, criminal activity.

  • Deepfakes and elections as well as people’s reputations.

  • Hallucinations.

  • Sycophancy.

  • Jailbreaking.

  • Bias in training data causing unrepresentative results.

  • Tendency of ‘Big Tech” to way overclaim capabilities of models.

  • Loss of control over personal data.

  • Privacy issues.

Safety has a similar a similar set of ongoing challenges:

  • Expanding hazard analysis to the new technological advances in engineering.

  • Incorporating social, psychological, and managerial factors into hazard analysis and accident investigation.

  • Extending linear causality models to non-linear causality concepts.

  • Reconciling the tensions between agile software development and assuring system properties such as safety.

  • Developing non-probabilistic approaches to risk assessment for non-stochastic system components.

  • Creating new approaches to system engineering to reduce up-front development costs for safety-critical systems.

Many challenges exist that span both safety and security. For example, such challenges include adapting our safety and security approaches to the increasing complexity of our engineered systems including:

  • Assuring safety and security when using AI, especially LLMs, which may mean that it is not used in critical systems.

  • Protecting against the use of AI to attack critical systems.

  • Identifying and handling the risks of taking humans out of the decision-making loop in critical systems.

  • Integrating human factors into the design and engineering of automated systems and designing for dynamic shared control of critical systems by humans and software.

  • Educational and training challenges for safety and security.

  • Creating approaches to building safety and security into automated systems from the beginning of development rather than relying on post-development assurance.

  • Integrating safety and security into widely used system engineering tools such as MBSE.

Designing safety, security, and other desired properties into software and systems from the beginning is of particular importance. Software in even common systems (such as automobiles) today can contain tens of millions of lines of code. A high level of assurance post-development is impossible. Our traditional approaches to assuring safety and security work only on completed code. We need new modeling and analysis that can be used to guide the development of our new complex systems and build desired qualities in from the beginning of development.

Final Thoughts

These are just some of our current and future challenges. More generally, we need to deal with the risks of the rapidly increasing complexity of engineered systems today, mostly due to the incorporation of computers. We are building intellectually unmanageable systems that defy the understanding by all but perhaps a handful of experts and our ability to predict how our creations will behave is diminishing. Indeed, complexity can be defined as intellectual unmanageability. Throughout history, inventions and new technology have often gotten ahead of their scientific underpinnings and engineering knowledge with the result being increased risk until science, engineering, and society caught up. We are now in that catch-up stage.

The importance of computers in every aspect of our world is far beyond what the pioneers in our field 70 years ago could have imagined. Our challenge today is, like that of Victor Frankenstein, to ensure we can control our creation and its impact on society. To do that, society in general and engineering in particular need our help. Computer scientists need to look beyond computers themselves to control the risks of our technology on the environments in which that technology is being used.

We may also need to develop new paradigms for managing risk. Many of the old paradigms rest on assumptions that are no longer true. Einstein’s admonition applies here: “We cannot solve our problems with the same thinking we used when we created them.” Computer scientists and others need to change the fundamental ways that we tackle risk issues to make significant progress.

I am looking forward to doing my part in promoting these new ways of thinking and tackling the difficult problems. Future Communications Inside Risks columns will examine what those new paradigms might entail.

item.title: AI Finds its Way Into Backcountry Search and Rescue
item.dc:creator: Karen Emslie
item.description: AI is transforming how search and rescue is carried out, and also enabling rescuers to build bespoke solutions for their teams.
item.content:encoded:
Encountering a drone during a revitalizing mountain hike can feel irksome and intrusive unless you are lost or injured; then, it just might save your life. Drone technologies and AI are increasingly vital components of search and rescue (SAR) assignments. In some cases, SAR efforts that previously took days can be reduced to hours. AI is not only transforming how SAR is carried out, but it is also enabling rescuers to build bespoke solutions for their teams.

A New Team Member

Think Colorado, think wilderness. The 103,717.5 sq. mi. state abounds with mountains, canyons, ravines, rivers, and forests; it has an average altitude of 6,800 ft., rising to a peak of 14,433 ft. at Mount Elbert. It is an outdoor enthusiast’s paradise. According to a report by market research firm Longwoods International, Colorado received 96.8 million visitors in 2025. In summer, millions of people safely enjoy activities like hiking, climbing, and whitewater rafting, but inevitably, some get lost or injured. Each year, the Colorado Search and Rescue Association (CSAR) responds to around 3,000 SAR incidents, which can also include urban SAR when, for example, a child or an Alzheimer’s patient becomes lost.

CSAR is an umbrella organization that coordinates volunteer SAR networks in the state, including Boulder Emergency Squad (BES), Rocky Mountain Rescue, and Front Range Rescue Dogs. Steve Lanaghen is a long-serving rescuer with the special tactics group of BES: “We’re a very multifaceted group,” he said. “We do water rescue, dive rescue, airplane crashes, backcountry search, urban search, law support, fire support.”

Lanaghen has witnessed how technology has changed SAR over the decades. “We’ve gone from using pencils and paper maps on the hood of a car to figure out where people are, to now having a mobile command center with multiple monitors and Starlink; we can stream video back into our emergency operations center in the city.”

BES has been using drones since 2013. They transformed SAR by enabling what Lanaghen called “a bird’s eye view” of a search area, while reducing risk by providing overwatch for rescuers in hazardous conditions, like steep vertical work or river rescues. Today, the squad’s fleet of drones is augmented by AI technologies like computer vision for anomaly detection and thermal imaging, which uses temperature variation to spot missing people in visually obscured areas, like forests.

Mike Kabjian, who works alongside Lanaghen at BES, sees AI as “a search team member that can do things we can’t.” Models can now analyze drone footage pixel-by-pixel in real time and identify subtle color, shape, or motion anomalies that could signal the location of a person. Kabjian pointed to software such as Eagle Eyes, which “draws a little circle on the screen when it sees a color that statistically shouldn’t be there,” he said. “We’re looking for a person, but it could also be a jacket, a shoe, a backpack.”

The squad also can analyze data from drone live streams, georeferenced aerials maps, and thermal imagery via tools like Nova Maps and ADIAT, and are working with a Boulder-based technology startup, Odin Autonomy, to automate and streamline the operation of swarms of drones on SAR missions.

Lanaghen sees no tension between technology and the outdoors. “We have a lot of people who are very comfortable in the woods and very comfortable behind a computer.” He keeps a keen eye on how the latest AI advances could improve SAR, flagging robotic olfaction or e-nose systems as “out there” but full of potential. Lanaghen said future SAR AI systems could be made up of multiple sensors working together: “Some super-mobile sensor that can fly, swim, crawl under rocks or whatever; that can sense all these different things. It’ll give us a completely different view of what’s out there.”

On a planet full of wilderness, it is unsurprising for AI SAR to have global reach. In June, Fire and Rescue New South Wales in Australia found two missing hikers in Kosciuszko National Park within five hours using an AI-powered drone. Meanwhile, Salvamont, Romania’s National Mountain Rescuers Association, has partnered with Vodafone to build an AI-powered SAR system that captures and analyzes geolocated images to find missing hikers and climbers. In research, a team from Glasgow University, Scotland, has developed a deep reinforcement learning model for optimizing drones’ search paths, and an Italian team has presented an automated object detection pipeline for finding people lost in forests using real-time thermal video.

The SAR Programmer

It is not only developers and researchers who are innovating AI for SAR. For Kabjian, one of the greatest impacts of AI on SAR is enabling non-technical rescuers to build solutions. Tools for de-confliction, that is, knowing the position of other drones in an area to avoid accidents, exist, but can be expensive or not an exact fit for a SAR team’s needs, so Kabjian built his own. Using AI as a programming assistant, he created a drone finder that plots positional data onto CalTopo, the backcountry map software the squad uses. Design of the hardware—external antenna on the command vehicle—also was assisted by AI. As Kabjian puts it, “AI’s not in the product, but AI built the product.”

It is an approach he and Lanaghen currently are deploying to design an SAR video streaming system that fits the squad’s specific technical and privacy needs. “We need it fed without any lag into our command vehicle,” said Kabjian. “Simultaneous to that, we need an encrypted stream going to the cloud, not using RTSP [Real-Time Streaming Protocol], but using SRT [Secure Reliable Transport].”

Another area ripe for improvement with AI is SAR management. Kabjian described “the madness that is the first hour of a search,” when information like a person’s description and where they might have gone need to be processed and rescuers are mustering. “There’s people talking to you, there’s trucks coming, and everybody’s excited to go do something. It’s cognitive overload,” he said. Kabjian and Lanaghen aim to make this process “a more efficient machine” by automating rescuer check-in and form filling, and using AI to carry out initial planning and suggest rescue assignments.

Despite enthusiastically embracing AI, both seasoned rescuers stressed they will always take a strict “human-in-the-loop” verification approach. Said Kabjian, “Our key focus is life safety, we won’t be able to turn that completely over to a computer. We need experienced rescuers’ eyes on it to make sure that no one is endangered by the technology’s decision-making.”

For many, time in the wilderness means a break from technology, but when it comes to search and rescue, an AI-loaded drone whirring overhead will likely to be very welcome.

Karen Emslie is a location-independent freelance journalist and essayist.
